articles.title_orig: Sixth person who had measles has died in Pennsylvania, local coroner says

articles.content_orig:

A sixth person infected with measles has died in Pennsylvania after the worst outbreak of the virus in the state in over 35 years.
The 39-year-old woman had underlying health conditions and had previously been treated for measles, the Franklin County Coroner’s Office said Monday.
“This is the first death in Franklin County in many years with a patient with a recent history of a measles diagnosis and meets the definition set forth by the Pennsylvania Department of Health for a measles-associated death ,” the coroner’s office wrote in a statement, shared to Facebook.
The office said it would not release any additional details about the case.
Measles is spreading across Pennsylvania and in other parts of the U.S. The state’s Department of Health reported 1,136 cases since the start of the year and 157 in the last week alone.
Pennsylvania’s measles tracker showed five deaths Monday but a note explained the next update would be Wednesday due to the Columbus Day and Indigenous Peoples’ Day holiday.
The state’s Health Department told The Independent it is aware of the death reported by the Franklin County coroner.
“Our team has reached out to the coroner’s office and is conducting a thorough review of the reported death. We will update the public after our investigation is finished,” Press Secretary Neil Ruhland said via email.
As part of the investigation, the department will rely on its definition for a measles-associated death, he noted.
The department defines a measles-associated death as one that occurs within 30 days of the start of symptoms of infection, with clinical evidence of an infection, a positive lab test for measles and no other unrelated causes.
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention only reports two deaths from measles in Pennsylvania.
There have been no updates to the federal death count since late September. A note above the data states the total is subject to change as more information becomes available and “relevant reviews are completed.”
Pennsylvania’s first measles death was reported in late August. It was also the first measles death of the year in the U.S.
Health Sec. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro have traded shots at each other on social media over the numbers.
Shapiro blasted what he called the Trump administration’s “incompetence” in responding to the virus and Kennedy initially claimed that Pennsylvania’s measles deaths were “ fabricated.”
The CDC previously told The Independent that the agency had "mounted an aggressive response to measles outbreaks across the country.”
“We are saddened to learn of this death in Pennsylvania. The CDC remains committed to supporting the state as it responds to the ongoing measles outbreak,” HHS Press Sec. Grace Davis Jamison said in an email to The Independent responding to a request for comment on the death count.
Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to recommend the MMR vaccine as the most effective way to prevent measles infection, she added.
There are 4,080 confirmed measles cases this year in the District of Columbia and 46 states. There have also been 42 new outbreaks in 2026.
Last year, there were 2,289 confirmed measles cases. Some outbreaks from 2025 continued into the beginning of this year, including in Utah and South Carolina.
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause life-threatening brain-swelling and high fever, especially in those who have not received two doses of the MMR vaccine.
Vaccination provides lifelong protection against infection and severe illness. But rising vaccine hesitancy and misinformation has led cases to reach the worst levels since the 1990s, doctors previously told The Independent .
The U.S. is now at risk of losing its long-held elimination status , medical experts say , because there has been continuous spread of measles for more than a year.

articles.title_orig: China Open prides itself on being a 'cradle of champions'
articles.title_zh: China Open prides itself on being a 'cradle of champions'
articles.content_orig:
In capturing the 2026 Women's China Open title this past weekend, 16-year-old amateur Liu Yujie joins an elite group of players who have won the country's national championship and used the tournament as a stepping stone to success in the wider golf world.
For Beijing native Liu, the daughter of former table tennis world champion and Olympic gold medalist Liu Guoliang, great things undoubtedly lay ahead after she made history in Shanghai as the first amateur to win the national championship.
"Winning the Women's China Open, such an important national-level tournament, means a lot to me," said Liu, 16th in the World Amateur Golf Ranking.
"It's a big event, and it also marks my third win on the CLPG Tour. I'm very happy to celebrate this moment with everyone."
Since its inception in 2006, when the tournament was played as the Orient China Ladies Open, the championship has become known as "the cradle of champions" — and it's easy to see why.
South Korean great Shin Ji-yai raised the trophy in that inaugural year, winning by a commanding eight strokes at Orient Xiamen. She would come back to successfully defend her title the following year, this time beating future world No 1 Tseng Ya-ni from Chinese Taipei by five strokes.
Shin would eventually take her game to the LPGA Tour where she would win two major tournaments and hold the world No 1 ranking for 25 weeks, the first Asian player to do so.
It was a pattern many Women's China Open winners would follow in the early years, as 2009 winner Ryu So-yeon would also rise to the top spot in the world rankings, winning two majors along the way.
Kim Hyo-joo, the current world No 4, first won the championship in 2012 as a teenager in Xiamen. Even while playing full-time on the LPGA Tour in later years, the Korean great would return to China, winning the national championship in 2014 and, again, in 2016 to become the only three-time winner. Fellow Korean Park Sung-hyun also won the tournament in 2015 and became the world No 1 on several occasions between 2017-2019, also winning two majors.
CLPG Tour founder TK Pen remembers those early years of the championship when South Korean players were dominating.
"The Women's China Open was founded in 2006 at a time when China's golf market was still in its early stages of development. In its first years, the event was independently funded by the organizers and co-sanctioned with the KLPGA Tour," said Pen, the CLPG Tour's chairman.
"Through that partnership, the tournament carried world ranking points from its inaugural edition and gave young players from the Chinese mainland and Taiwan the opportunity to compete alongside leading Korean professionals."
Feng Shanshan, who was the Chinese No 1 at the time and a regular on the LPGA Tour, played in those early championships, determined to win her national championship.
Facing an elite field of top Koreans each year, a runner-up finish to Kim Hye-youn in 2011 was the closest she got to achieving her goal.
Feng, who retired in 2022 after an outstanding career in which she won 25 tournaments worldwide, won the bronze medal at the 2016 Rio Olympics and was ranked the world's No 1 player for six months between 2017 and 2018, said the experiences she gained playing in her national championship played a "pivotal role" in shaping the player she became.
"In the early days, competing against strong Korean players showed us just how high the standard was, and it motivated me to work harder, stay resilient and keep striving for success," said the Guangzhou native and winner of the 2012 Women's PGA Championship.
"I am proud to see Chinese golfers achieving success on the LPGA Tour, and I believe the future of women's golf in China is exceptionally bright. Today, we have a growing pool of talented amateurs excelling on the CLPG Tour and winning tournaments, which bodes well for the years ahead. I am confident the next decade will be a remarkable era for women's golf in China."
With the tournament dormant in 2017 and no longer a co-sponsored event with the KLPGA Tour, the event returned the following year as a CLPG Tour event with hopes high that it would produce its first champion from the Chinese mainland.
But it wasn't to be then, as Lee Min of Chinese Taipei became the first cross-Strait winner of the championship with her 2018 victory in Xiamen.
Much like the men's US Open, which didn't produce a homegrown winner until year 17 of the championship, it took until 2019, when Lin Xiyu finally broke through to win the Women's China Open by two strokes over Liu Yan in Xiamen. After the tournament returned to the CLPG Tour calendar in 2023 following the pandemic, Lin's victory would open the door for more Chinese winners — Ye Lei (2023), Ji Yuai (2024) and Pang Runzhi last year — to raise the trophy.
"That achievement will always hold a special place in my heart, and I am proud to have contributed to the growth of our country's golfing history," said Guangdong native Lin who won a record seven times on the CLPG Tour.
"From the time I began competing, the Women's China Open stood out as one of the most important tournaments on the calendar. It inspired me to push harder and strive for excellence. Like all great national opens, it has played a pivotal role in developing women's golf and providing a stage for Chinese players to challenge themselves."
Wei Qingfeng, secretary-general of the China Golf Association, credited those early years of cooperating with the KLPGA Tour as a catalyst in helping to establish the "tournament experience" in the country.
"It gave Chinese golf a more direct view of the standards of the global women's game and helped accelerate progress in tournament operations, competition management and media promotion. In that sense, the Women's China Open became an important doorway through which Chinese women's golf — and Chinese golf more broadly — could begin to engage more closely with the world."
With the Women's China Open firmly established, as a national open carrying the country's name, Wei said the tournament now had a broader responsibility to strengthen its domestic identity, establish a strong position in Asia and attract more leading players from around the world.
"Achieving that goal will require continued progress in commercial value, prize money, international participation and schedule coordination, while also drawing strength from the growing depth of China's young and professional player pool," he said.
"The long-term ambition is clear: to help more Chinese players progress from this stage to the world, while continuing to elevate the Women's China Open toward the level of leading national championships internationally."
Founder Pen added that, with the emergence of a new generation of players led by Yin Ruoning, the world No 6 who won three times on the CLPG Tour as a teenager, it has further highlighted the value of high-level international competition in player development. Looking ahead, he said, international expansion remained a "key priority" for the CLPG Tour.
"Rather than focusing only on bringing top players into China, the longer-term ambition is for the CLPG Tour to expand outward, particularly into Southeast Asia, creating a more stable competitive pathway for young Asian professionals and strengthening the position of the Women's China Open within the regional and global women's golf landscape," said Pen.
For young players such as Zhou Shiyuan, a three-time winner on the CLPG Tour before turning pro in February, this is undoubtedly good news. The Chongqing teenager noted the championship also served as an important training ground for pros and amateurs alike who have ambitions to take their game to a higher level in the greater golf world.
"The Women's China Open is one of the most prestigious events for every Chinese golfer. To compete in this event is not only about honor, but also about responsibility and dreams — it truly is the highest form of recognition," said Zhou, who finished equal

articles.title_orig: Trump faces stiff bipartisan pushback to Russian diesel import deal
articles.title_zh: Trump faces stiff bipartisan pushback to Russian diesel import deal
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump is trying to make America more like him.
But voters will soon get to deliver a verdict on the president’s efforts to redefine how the government he leads wields power at home and abroad.
Three flashpoints illustrate how his coercive and transactional instincts are changing the character of the country and how the rest of the world sees us.
Ever since World War II, America has nurtured democracy. But by allowing Russia to supply markets with diesel , Trump will reward a ruthless authoritarian, President Vladimir Putin, who is killing scores of Ukrainian civilians as he aims to crush their independence.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the death by firing squad of the Fort Hood mass shooter meanwhile risks putting the United States in the category of Iran, the Taliban and Hamas in carrying out public executions.
And the shooting by federal agents in New York last week of a citizen of the Dominican Republic while a 5-year-old was in the car was the government’s latest flex of violent force in public in an intensifying deportation crackdown.
Each event sparked a political backlash, and each raises questions about the unconstrained use of presidential authority and how eroded legal and behavioral standards will ultimately sit with the national conscience.
But each also directly flows from the personality of a president who made no secret of his intentions when he was twice chosen by voters in democratic elections and who represents the views of tens of millions of citizens.
The midterm elections are being dominated by high prices for food and housing, a backlash against AI data centers , and public fury over the Iran war.
But the election also marks 10 years since Trump first won power, and it will serve indirectly as an accounting of his attempts to define 21st century national greatness through a prism of his truculent and idiosyncratic values.
Growing concerns about the Russia diesel deal , a potentially livestreamed execution and Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity may hint at Trump’s eroded political clout nearly halfway through his second term.
And the shift of the electoral calendar to a presidential cycle in a few weeks will begin a debate on whether Trump’s redefinition of American exceptionalism is an aberration or whether it will linger in his image when he’s left office.
Trump’s deal with Putin to send diesel onto international markets is a blunt demonstration of “America First” in action and the US president’s tendency to use foreign policy to promote his political goals.
The move shatters the international sanctions regime that battered Russia’s economy after the invasion of Ukraine; delivers a huge propaganda victory to Putin; and reflects the US president’s pattern of accommodating the Kremlin strongman.
It deals a new blow to the morale of Ukrainian civilians, who are under escalating Russian attacks, including at least 33 who died when two public buses were targeted .
It opens a huge rift with NATO allies at a moment when Moscow is accused of a campaign of sabotage, harassment and airspace violations in Europe. The Dutch defense minister last week branded Russia “our enemy.”
And Trump’s demand Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky — a key Moscow condition — will renew fears that he’s siding with Kremlin war aims. Those fears were also recently exacerbated by Trump’s failure to license Kyiv to produce Patriot missiles .
But there is a logical explanation for Trump’s decision.
He’s in a political and economic bind because the cost of diesel has hit record levels, hammering US agriculture and raising food prices. Most of this is because of his war in Iran, and it is unclear whether the deal will lower prices quickly. But he had a burning domestic political imperative to do more, whatever the expense.
“It’s another example of our president thinking out of the box,” House Majority Whip Tom Emmer told ABC News’ “This Week” on Sunday. Emmer added: “Our president is trying to find every answer possible to help the American people.”
But former Vice President Mike Pence balked at easing the economic vise on Russia. “America should not be throwing a lifeline to Putin’s war machine. Now is the time to stand strong against Russian aggression as we did during the first Trump administration,” Pence wrote in a post on X.
Trump rejects the kind of hawkish, traditional Republicanism that Pence represents. The president has a narrower definition of national and personal interest: On the same day he delivered a huge win for Putin, an accused war criminal, and again warned he may destroy Iran, Trump slammed his latest Nobel Peace Prize snub as “an embarrassment” and “disgraceful.”
Nidal Hasan is a US Army major convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder for targeting soldiers headed to Afghanistan. The question is not whether his victims deserve justice following a judicial process. It’s whether staging a public execution would infringe constitutional protections; whether it is consistent with America’s modern values; and if it would hand Hasan the martyrdom he sought.
Hegseth explained last week that the execution would be public because “people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The defense secretary favors the performative use of force and is contemptuous toward those who fear it violates American principles. He has, for example, defended US strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific that have killed at least 221 people and that critics call unconstitutional extrajudicial assassinations.
A backlash could still scupper the livestream execution plan. Trump said over the weekend that he will decide whether it will happen.
But opponents worry that going ahead will stain America’s moral reputation and reward extremist groups with a propaganda triumph.
“What is he mimicking, ISIS executions?” Connecticut Sen. Chris Murphy told CNN’s Erin Burnett on Thursday. “I understand that in this country we have the death penalty, but public executions is medieval.”
Some Republicans are also concerned. “I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that,” said Georgia Rep. Austin Scott. And Utah Sen. John Curtis warned on X , “A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment.”
The public use of military-style force in law enforcement and a narrative of governmental toughness also underpins the deportation crackdown. It has come with grave consequences, including the deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota.
In the latest controversy, Oscar Belgal, 28, from the Dominican Republic, suffered a superficial wound to the neck when he was shot by immigration agents in the Bronx last week. His child was not physically injured. Federal authorities said officers believed that their lives were in danger. The injured man had previously pleaded guilty to fourth-degree grand larceny and received five years of probation, according to court records.
Critics see such confrontations as unacceptable examples of untamed federal government power. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the officers involved were not wearing uniforms and that ICE agents are “making the city terrified.”
But Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNN’s Jake Tapper on “State of the Union” on Sunday that Belgal was to blame. “The truth is this guy was an awful human being. He was a thug. He was a gangbanger,” Mullin said. He placed the blame on Belgal for putting his child at risk: “The last thing I would have done is put my son or one of my kids in danger.”
Mullin’s comments are consistent with the views of many Americans who favor stronger immigration enforcement and who responded to Trump’s searing promises to launch law and order crackdowns in his campaigns.

articles.title_orig: China Mobile triples capacity at mega Inner Mongolia computing hub amid AI push
articles.title_zh: China Mobile triples capacity at mega Inner Mongolia computing hub amid AI push
articles.content_orig:
The US$403 million expansion covers 44,500 square metres, equivalent to six soccer fields, and boasts a total power capacity of 120 megawatts
The expansion of its data centre in Hohhot was recently completed, with total processing capacity increased to 20,100 petaflops, according to a report by Inner Mongolia Daily on Monday.
That was triple its previous capacity of 6,700 petaflops, according to data from a 2024 report by the state-run People’s Posts and Telecommunications News.
A petaflop is a measurement of a computer’s speed and is equal to a quadrillion operations per second. Of that total, 16,700 petaflops were dedicated to artificial intelligence and smart computing tasks, the Monday report said.

This copy is for your personal, non-commercial use only. Distribution and use of this material are governed by

https://www.wsj.com/politics/policy/ken-paxton-texas-senate-dubai-trip-b54292c3
As President Trump weighed endorsing Ken Paxton over incumbent Texas Sen. John Cornyn this spring, he was told that damaging revelations were likely to surface about Paxton, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump was dismissive and said there would be more negative material about Democratic nominee James Talarico.
Trump plowed ahead and endorsed the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general, helping him win the Republican-primary runoff in May. Months later, that decision is looking like Trump’s biggest gamble of the midterms.
Despite efforts by Paxton to paint his opponent as a far-left zealot, Talarico consistently holds a narrow lead in polls, raising a once unthinkable possibility: A Democrat could win statewide office in Texas for the first time since 1994.
Meanwhile, damaging revelations about Paxton continue to emerge. A new scene that could join the list: a previously unreported New Year’s Eve 2024 celebration where Paxton partied in Dubai with two fugitives from U.S. justice and a woman who wasn’t his wife.
As fireworks exploded over the Burj Khalifa skyscraper to welcome 2025, Paxton and his girlfriend Tracy Duhon watched from a luxury high-rise balcony full of people, according to a video of the gathering reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, details of which were contained in court filings and confirmed by people familiar with the matter.
Among those at the event with Texas’ top law-enforcement official were two Americans who had been indicted months before on federal healthcare-fraud charges but failed to return to the U.S., Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, according to the court records and people familiar with the matter. Ahmed, a healthcare executive, had donated $190,000 to Paxton, campaign finance records show, including $25,000 days after he was indicted.

articles.title_orig: China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behind
articles.title_zh: China reduced extreme poverty fast, but Indonesia hasn’t been far behind
articles.content_orig:
China is often the poster child for rapid reductions in poverty, and for good reason. In the early 1980s, over 90% of its population lived in extreme poverty, but by the early 2020s, that number had dropped to nearly zero.
Some might assume that China is the only reason why global extreme poverty has declined. But that’s wrong : many countries have seen dramatic reductions in poverty, too. Indonesia is one clear example; it’s shown alongside China on the chart.
In 1984, 86% of Indonesians lived on less than $3 per day. By 2025, this had fallen to less than 4%. While it didn’t quite match China’s decline, it has still been impressive. The number of people living in extreme poverty has fallen from 140 million to about 10 million.
Note that the international poverty line is extremely low, defined as people living on less than $3 per day. But Indonesia has also made progress when measuring higher poverty lines .
Many of us will have seen the stark images of plastic in the ocean: bottles and wrappers clumped together, or rubbish trapped along the coastline. But how much of the world’s plastic waste ends up in the ocean?
In 2020, Gapminder asked people in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark, and the UK this question. They had three options to choose from:
Almost nine in ten people picked B or C, thinking it was more than one-third.
The correct answer was A: around 0.5% of plastic waste ends up in the ocean.
The chart shows how the OECD gets to this number. Globally, we produce around 350 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. Most of this is managed responsibly, either in secure landfills, through recycling, or incineration. But around one-quarter of it is mismanaged or littered.
From there, a decreasing fraction of plastic waste leaks to the environment, then into rivers and coastlines, and finally into the ocean. Around 1.7 million tonnes end up there: around 0.5% of what was generated in the first place.
People tend to think that most of our plastic ends up there, but only a tiny percentage does. This should make plastic pollution an easier problem to solve: we already know how to manage most of it well. The challenge is to ensure that all plastic is handled this way.
The new Living Planet Index report has just been published. It estimates an average decline of 73% in studied wildlife populations since 1970. You can see this in the chart.
Every two years, it hits the headlines, and I always have mixed feelings about it.
I love that biodiversity loss gets its rare spot in the limelight. It’s a problem that I think doesn’t get enough attention. The trouble is that journalists often report it incorrectly: either as the number of animals or wildlife lost, the number of species in decline, or the number that have gone extinct.
But it tells us none of that.
It examines changes across nearly 36,000 animal populations and reports the average change. This gets even more complicated because it’s based on a geometric mean, and populations get weighted differently in the final index.
When we look a bit deeper, we see that not all populations are doing poorly. As shown in the chart, around half have declined, while the other half have either increased in abundance or remained stable.
As I explained in a previous article , being able to identify which of these populations is doing particularly badly is crucial if we’re to focus our conservation efforts on where they’re needed most.
In 1950, almost one in four children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. In Africa, one in three children died.
The chart shows the change since then. In every region, the mortality rate of children has declined.
In Africa and Oceania, the child mortality rate declined 5-fold, in Asia 10-fold, and in Europe about 27-fold.
Progress was not always steady. The sharp spike in Asia around 1960 was due to the “Great Leap Forward” famine in Mao’s China, the deadliest famine in recorded history.
And the progress is far from finished. The global average has declined to 3.5%, but this still means that about 4.7 million children younger than five years died in 2025 — 13,000 children every single day.
Globally, electricity generation per person has grown by more than 50% this century.
In the United Kingdom, things have moved in the opposite direction. Its generation per person peaked in 2003 and has fallen by more than a third since then.
You can see this in the chart, which shows generation per person since 1920. Today, levels are back to where they were in the late 1960s.
Some of that decline is a change in electricity imports, rather than demand: net imports have increased from 1% of electricity demand in 2010 to 9% in 2025. But it’s still true that the UK consumes much less electricity than it used to.
The most common explanation is deindustrialization: as the economy shifted from manufacturing to services, electricity demand fell. That’s part of the explanation, but far from all of it.
Sectoral data from the International Energy Agency confirms that electricity consumption in industry has fallen by one-quarter since 2005 (more if we calculate this per person). But residential and commercial electricity use has fallen by just as much.
Deindustrialization has reduced demand, but improvements in energy efficiency — such as the shift from incandescent to LED lightbulbs and the introduction of efficiency standards for appliances — have played an important role too.
The median age of a country or region is the age that divides its population into two equal parts: half of the people are older, and half are younger. As the population ages, the median age rises.
That’s what this chart tracks. It shows how the median age has changed across world regions from 2000 to 2023, the most recent year for which the UN publishes estimates.
The first thing that stands out is perhaps the least surprising: some regions have much older populations than others. Africa is very young: half of its population is younger than 19. Europe is much older: half of its population is over 42.
But there’s a second point that I think receives less attention in public discussions: how quickly this is changing. Of the six world regions, Latin America is where the median age has increased the most since 2000. It rose by a third, from 23 to 31 years, in a bit less than a generation.
Europe’s population is older, but the median age has been rising more quickly in Latin America this century. That’s largely due to fertility falling later and faster in the latter.
Hannah Ritchie and Pablo Arriagada
When people think about global oil, their minds often go toward countries in the Middle East.
But it’s the United States that is the world’s largest oil producer.
The chart shows oil production by country since 1990. As you can see, the US has been the largest producer for the last nine years, since it overtook Saudi Arabia.
Production in the US gradually declined during the 1990s and early 2000s, then increased sharply after 2010 and is now at an all-time high.
This data comes from the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy .

articles.title_orig: Republicans Promoted a False Rumor That James Talarico Was in Ohio
articles.title_zh: Republicans Promoted a False Rumor That James Talarico Was in Ohio
articles.content_orig:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's campaign shared security camera footage with CBS News that appears to show Talarico at his home in Texas for the first eight days of this month — pushing back on claims that Talarico was hiding the reasons for his disappearance.
Talarico was absent from the campaign trail for almost two weeks, saying he caught a bad case of the flu. The disappearance drew criticism and speculation from his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.
But on Monday, Talarico's campaign shared a set of security camera images that they say show the state lawmaker and Democratic candidate at his home in Texas every day from Oct. 1 to Oct. 8, one day before Talarico made a public appearance.
The eight timestamped images — which include watermarks from home security camera company SimpliSafe — appeared to have been taken from a camera in the backyard of Talarico's house in the state capital of Austin. CBS News matched features in the backyard to recent satellite imagery of Talarico's address. Though low resolution, the photos show a male figure with brown hair at various times of day and wearing different outfits.
The images were first reported by The New York Times .
The mental health facility at the center of the conspiracy theories, Lindner Center of Hope in Mason, Ohio, also wrote on social media that Talarico "has never received treatment" there.
Talarico campaign spokesman J.T. Ennis said in a statement that claims Talarico was elsewhere were "a lie designed to promote a pathetic conspiracy theory."
"Last week James Talarico was home in Austin, Texas recovering from the flu," Ennis said.

articles.title_orig: Calls Show How Confusion Delayed Emergency Response for Christa Pike
articles.title_zh: Calls Show How Confusion Delayed Emergency Response for Christa Pike
articles.content_orig:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV) - What happened the night Christa Pike’s attempted execution failed? Authorities have released the transcript of the 911 call made from Riverbend Maximum Security Institution that night, providing new details about what occurred.
Metro Nashville Emergency Communications Center (DEC) released the transcript on Monday — a little over one week after the botched execution .
The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications (DEC) first received notification of the incident at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution through a 911 call at 8:40 p.m. CT on Sept. 30, 2026.
DEC said following a review by Metro Legal, it was determined that the original 911 audio call is exempt from public disclosure under Tennessee Code § 10-7-504(h).
“While recognizing this exemption, DEC has made a good-faith effort to provide additional information by preparing a written account of the initial call based on a review of the audio recording,” a spokesperson for DEC said.
The written account was released below:
The failed attempt happened after a day of back-and-forth amongst courts about whether the procedure would proceed.
Pike was scheduled to be executed at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution the morning of Sept. 30, but shortly before, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ordered that her execution be paused.
The pause was issued because the court believed that she should be allowed to challenge the legality of her sentence. Pike’s attorneys then asked the U.S. Supreme Court to maintain that pause while a federal appeals court reviewed a new legal challenge.
That evening, the Supreme Court said in a 6-3 decision that the execution would be allowed to proceed. She would have been the first woman in more than 200 years to be executed in Tennessee. She is the only woman on death row in the state.
But things went wrong when they attempted to administer the two doses of pentobarbital.
“The vein in my arm feels like it’s about to bust,” witnesses heard Pike say as she was undergoing lethal injection.
The state administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be lethal. But witnesses and her attorneys say that they did not have the intended effect. Instead, one witness said, “heavy snoring is the best description we can get you for the noises she was making.”
Shortly after, WSMV observed ambulances arriving at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution and leaving soon after, followed by police.
Pike was taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center.
Attorneys later confirmed that she was unconscious and on a ventilator. It was revealed that on Oct. 5, her attorneys and medical team believed she was brain dead and would be taken off life support within the days.
But she regained consciousness the following morning.
“I do not have an explanation for what happened between Monday night and Tuesday morning, but what we do know is that Christa has a long road to recovery ,” one of her attorneys, Randy Spivey, said.
Pike’s attorneys announced on Saturday that she had been released from the hospital and was returned to the Deborah K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center where she has been housed for more than 30 years.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.
The case revealed that Pike, who was 18 at the time, worked with 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp and 18-year-old Shadolla Peterson to plan and carry out the killing, which became known as the “Jobs Corps Murder.” Pike and Slemmer had both been Jobs Corps members at the time of the murder, which took place on the University of Tennessee campus.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville Police Chief during the 1995 murder, described it as “ an incredibly grotesque crime scene , one of the most brutal I’ve ever seen.”
According to Keith, Pike had tortured Slemmer for nearly an hour with a box cutter, “carving a pentagram on her chest before she crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.”
Pike’s lawyers have argued that her upbringing was not given enough consideration in her case. According to her defense, Pike was a victim of child abuse and multiple rapes, details they say were kept from the jury during her trial.
Tennessee previously claimed Pike was lying about her childhood, but has since acknowledged the abuse in open court.
For Keith, the upbringing is not an excuse.
“If everyone that had an abusive lifestyle killed someone, there’d be a lot more murders in this country,” he said. “This is not about how she’s become reformed, or that those days are past. Her values or morals have been set for a long time, and somewhere along the way, they got twisted.”
While Keith said that Pike never showed any remorse for the crime, Pike’s friend, Misty Armstrong, said otherwise.
According to Armstrong, Pike spent much of her time in prison trying to help other inmates .
“It took years of therapy for her to get there, but she did,” she said. “She changed and became a completely different person.”

articles.title_orig: Dr Fradley on Real-World Atrial Fibrillation and Cardiovascular Outcomes in CLL
articles.title_zh: Dr Fradley on Real-World Atrial Fibrillation and Cardiovascular Outcomes in CLL
articles.content_orig:
Michael G. Fradley, MD, discusses real-world data on atrial fibrillation incidence and its cardiovascular and health care impact in CLL.
Michael G. Fradley, MD, a professor of clinical medicine (cardiovascular medicine), section chief of Consultative Cardiology, and medical director of the Thalheimer Center for Cardio-Oncology at Penn Medicine, discussed real-world data presented on the incidence of atrial fibrillation (AFib) in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), and its effect on cardiovascular outcomes and health care resource utilization.
In a retrospective study , data from which were presented at the 2026 ASCO Annual Meeting , Fradley and colleagues used the US Symphony Health open claims database, which captures both privately insured and Medicare populations, Fradley explained. Among 233,362 patients with newly diagnosed CLL/SLL, 13.1% developed AFib within 1 year of diagnosis. Baseline characteristics did not differ significantly between patients who did and did not develop AFib, he noted.
However, patients who developed AFib (n = 30,518) had higher rates of stroke (14.3% vs 8.9%), bleeding events (27.9% vs 19.1%), and heart failure (54.5% vs 18.9%) than those who did not (n = 202,844; all, P < .0001).
In an exploratory analysis of 22,636 patients who started frontline treatment with a BTK inhibitor, Fradley noted that prior data suggest that AFib rates are highest with the first-generation agent ibrutinib (Imbruvica) and lower with acalabrutinib (Calquence) and zanubrutinib (Brukinsa). In this cohort, AFib occurred in 16.0% of patients treated with ibrutinib (n = 15,325), 13.0% of those treated with acalabrutinib (n = 5447), and 11.0% of those treated with zanubrutinib (n = 1864; P < .0001). The analysis is not definitive but is hypothesis generating, he added.
The lower AFib rate with zanubrutinib also translated to fewer cardiovascular adverse effects among patients who developed AFib, according to Fradley. Among patients with AFib, 4.8% of those treated with zanubrutinib had a stroke vs 12.2% of those treated with ibrutinib.
Fradley also highlighted the resource utilization findings, noting that AFib places a significant financial burden on the health care system. Patients with CLL who developed AFib had significantly greater outpatient, inpatient, and other medical service use than those who did not ( P < .0001).

Growers of giant pumpkins and their colossal gourds will gather on Monday in Northern California for an annual weighing competition, vying for the top award and a chance to challenge a world record set just last week in England .
At least 30 growers have registered for the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco , according to event spokesman Ronan Fowler.
Among those competing is four-time champion Travis Gienger, a horticulture teacher from Minnesota whose winning run ended last year when he couldn't enter because his pumpkin split while still growing.
Gienger, who navigated freezing temperatures this growing season, produced a pumpkin with a circumference large enough to make it a potential world-record contender, Fowler said.
Fowler mentioned last week that Gienger and his father intended to alternate behind the wheel during a 30-hour drive over the weekend to deliver the small-car-sized pumpkin to California.
Ian Paton of Lymington, on the southern coast of England, set the existing world record with a giant squash weighing 2,857 pounds (1,296 kilograms). That figure exceeds the combined weight of two-and-a-half concert grand pianos.
Paton raises his massive gourds in a greenhouse, while Gienger cultivates his entries in a backyard pumpkin patch in Anoka, a city along the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis , Fowler noted.
"The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable," the spokesman said.
Brandon Dawson, a resident of Santa Rosa , California, who won first place last year with a massive pumpkin weighing 2,346 pounds (1,064 kilograms), will also compete in the contest.
The winning grower this year will earn $9 for each pound of pumpkin and will have their giant gourd displayed during a parade through Half Moon Bay over the weekend. Should the winning entry surpass the world record, the competitor will receive an additional $30,000 prize.
Monday's proceedings, which mark the beginning of the city's autumn celebrations, will also feature a special appearance by pumpkin carver Mike Valladao.
However, these giant gourds are grown for size rather than flavor, so no oversized pumpkin pies will be served at the end of the event.

articles.title_orig: U.K. prime minister accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.title_zh: U.K. prime minister accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has said Russia did interfere with the Brexit referendum and warned that similar activities were taking place in France and Germany.
The prime minister told The Rest is Politics podcast that upon arriving in No 10, he had asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 vote, adding: "I've had the clear answer that, yes, there was."
"I think we've been too much on the back foot on that actually and we haven't informed people sufficiently about the extent to which people are seeking to disrupt the political process from overseas," he added.
Burnham did not provide further details about the type or extent of Moscow's activity during the Brexit referendum.
Asked about the prime minister's comments on BBC Breakfast, Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty said he wouldn't "get into specifics" of Russian interference in the 2016 vote when pushed for evidence.
"Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes," Doughty told the BBC. "They're engaged in information warfare, they're spending £1.5bn this year alone on disinformation and propaganda."
Doughty also denied that Burnham was raising the issue of Russian interference in the Brexit referendum because he wants to rejoin the EU.
He said: "This is a broader point he is making about Russian attempts to destabilise and interfere in our democracy."
Britain Unbound, a pro-Brexit campaign group, said Burnham's comments were "another crude attempt to undermine the legitimacy of the decision that the British people made in 2016".
It said that foreign interference in UK elections was "obviously unacceptable" but added: "There is no good reason to believe that Russian intervention influenced the outcome of the referendum in 2016.
"It is also insulting to suggest that voters were so easily duped."
In his interview, due to be released on Monday, Burnham said he had discussed the problem of Russian interference with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during his visit to Germany earlier this week.
"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics," he said.
He continued: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and I believe help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia."
It is the first time a UK prime minister has said Russia sought to sway the 2016 Brexit poll but there have long been warnings about efforts by the Kremlin to exert influence on UK politics.
In 2020, Parliament's Intelligence and Security Committee published a report into Russian interventions in UK elections and referendums.
It did not provide a definitive conclusion on whether Russia had attempted to influence the results of the EU referendum but did criticise successive governments for failing to fully assess or counter the threat.
In response, the Russian foreign minister dismissed the report out of hand and called it "Russophobia".
And a Kremlin spokesman said Russia did not meddle in other countries' elections.
In the same year, however, the then-Conservative government said it was "almost certain that Russian actors sought to interfere" in the 2019 general election.
BBC Verify has tracked Russian-linked disinformation campaigns including using AI to create fake videos which impersonate journalists and news organisations reporting on Ukraine.
One fake news website falsely claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had bought a mansion owned by King Charles at a discounted price.
Earlier this year, Vijay Rangarajan, head of the UK Electoral Commission, told MPs that Russian deepfake videos had been "used extensively in elections around the world".
"There is no reason to assume Britain would be an exception," he added.
Last month, during his speech to the United Nations, Burnham accused Russian agencies of using "every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears".
He announced that the UK would set up a new centre to "stem the poisonous tide" of disinformation.
A Downing Street spokesperson said: "We are focused on ensuring our citizens and our institutions are protected from foreign powers and their proxies seeking to threaten lives and undermine our democratic values.
"We are doing this by strengthening our powers through the National Security Act, strengthening the resilience of our institutions and critical national infrastructure, strengthening our borders, and strengthening our police and intelligence agencies."

articles.title_orig: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.title_zh: Trump blew past deadline to halt running taxpayer-funded campaign-style ads
articles.content_orig:
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.
An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social .
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."
The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.
The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.
The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.
The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."
Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.
"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."
The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.
It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US
articles.title_zh: One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US
articles.content_orig:
Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop
One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia , according to police.
The incident took place a Six Flags Over Georgia , about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department. The Cobb county police department said its detectives would investigate the circumstances of the incident.
Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citing eyewitnesses and anonymous local officials .
The rollercoaster, which was introduced at the park in 2006, has a top speed of 70mph (110km/h) and a 175ft drop.
A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident.
“We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said.
Local TV stations showed video of passengers being evacuated from the Goliath coaster. The rollercoaster, which was opened in 2006, goes up to 70mph (113kph) and reaches heights of 200 feet (61 meters), the park’s website reports.
Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week.

articles.title_orig: Trump ‘looking at’ firing Athens ambassador Guilfoyle over alleged plea for cash
articles.title_zh: Trump ‘looking at’ firing Athens ambassador Guilfoyle over alleged plea for cash
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is weighing firing the US ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, following reports of her alleged improper behaviour in Athens, which she has denied.
Asked if he was considering sacking her, Trump told reporters at the White House: "We're looking at it. Yeah, we're not happy." She is the ex-fiancée of the president's son, Donald Trump Jr.
The Wall Street Journal reported Guilfoyle allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration.
Her lawyers denied any wrongdoing by Guilfoyle and said she was owed the money for speaking engagements and consulting work for the donor.
Guilfoyle, 57, a former Fox News host and ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was appointed as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
At the time, Trump said "her extensive experience and leadership in law, media and politics, along with her sharp intellect make her supremely qualified" to represent the US abroad.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by the Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Deters never sent the money. Guilfoyle's lawyers have disputed the authenticity of the messages.
They said in a two-page statement on 12 October that Deters owed Guilfoyle about $150,000 for speeches and consulting work that she performed for him long before her ambassadorship.
"Asking a client to pay for work already done is not corruption. It is the opposite of corruption," they said.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle boasting of her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Democrats on the Senate and House foreign affairs committees have been calling on the state department to investigate her conduct in Greece.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured with Guilfoyle last week during his trip to Athens, was also reported to be unhappy with her in light of the allegations.
A former prosecutor in San Francisco and Los Angeles, she joined Fox News in 2006.
After leaving broadcasting in 2018, she joined the Trump campaign. The same year, she began a relationship with Donald Jr, and the couple eventually became engaged.
The pair reportedly parted ways in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.
Donald Jr wed socialite and model Bettina Anderson last year in Florida.

articles.title_orig: US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad
articles.title_zh: US archbishop says Catholics in army should not participate in firing squad
articles.content_orig:
United States Archbishop Timothy Broglio has urged Catholics who are members of the country’s armed forces not to take part in a planned public execution by firing squad, saying that it violates the teachings of the church.
Broglio released a strongly worded statement on Monday raising a series of concerns about the US military’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army major who killed 13 people during a shooting attack at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.
“I oblige any Catholics assigned to the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the Church,” Broglio said.
He also asked whether the US wants to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.
The plan to livestream the execution on December 3 was announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who characterised the spectacle as deterrence.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there are serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told the right-wing media outlet Real America’s Voice.
But the proposal has sparked backlash from lawmakers , rights groups and critics who warn that a publicly broadcast killing is not only unethical but could also be used as anti-US propaganda.
Hasan, now aged 56, was shot by the police during the 2009 Fort Hood attack and is now wheelchair-bound. Critics fear livestreaming Hasan’s death could turn him into a symbol for armed groups that may be hostile to the US.
Cardinal Blase J Cupich, the archbishop of Chicago, also condemned the plan to livestream the execution in a social media post on Monday, questioning the example it could set for children.
“Capital punishment is unacceptable in any case,” he said. “The planned broadcast of the taking of a life by firing squad is nothing short of performative barbarism. Do we really want our children, who will inevitably view it, exposed to the pornography of a state-sponsored slaying?”
Hegseth has said he wants the execution to take place at the same time and location as the 2009 shooting spree, and described using military members to carry out the death penalty.
“It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that,” Hegseth said of the firing squad. “Well, I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win.”
The last US military execution by firing squad was of Eddie Slovik, who was accused of desertion in 1945. He was the only US soldier to have such a sentence carried out for abandoning his post.
In Monday’s statement, Broglio also questioned the reasoning behind putting service members on camera to carry out Hasan’s death. He hinted that it could harm the US military’s image abroad.
“The US military generally enjoys a good reputation in the world,” Broglio wrote. “Is there really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man in a wheel chair to the whole world?”
Without mentioning Hasan’s case specifically, Pope Leo also released a statement on Saturday condemning the death penalty.
“The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person,” he said in a social media post.
“The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”
President Donald Trump , who oversaw an unprecedented spike in federal executions during his first term in office, has approved Hasan’s execution.
Still, on Saturday, he indicated that he has not decided whether to proceed with a livestream.
“There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters. “I’ll make a decision.”
Since the start of his second term as president, Trump has pushed for the increased use of the federal death penalty. In April, he also approved additional methods to carry out the death penalty, including the firing squad.
In the past, Trump has also floated the death penalty as a punishment for crimes ranging from drug dealing to sedition, a term he has invoked against political rivals .

articles.title_orig: U.S. and NATO commander vows to thwart Moscow, warns Kyiv over refinery strikes
articles.title_zh: U.S. and NATO commander vows to thwart Moscow, warns Kyiv over refinery strikes
articles.content_orig:
Professor Azeem Ibrahim says Russia’s heavily militarized Baltic enclave has become a testing ground for hybrid warfare targeting European infrastructure.
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that what he called the "lethal alliance" would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault.
"Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us," U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich said at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland , in an apparent warning to Moscow.
"This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force," he said during a panel titled "Theory of Victory: How Do We Achieve Military Success Against Russia in Deterrence and Defence?" on the first day of the forum.
US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS
NATO's top military commander warned Monday that the alliance would destroy "anything and everything" supporting an attack on allied territory and "break" enemy warfighting systems to thwart any potential future Russian assault. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Grynkewich, NATO's supreme allied commander in Europe, also outlined a three-pronged strategy of "blocking, blunting and breaking" enemy forces, making clear that while NATO is a defensive alliance, it is prepared to respond decisively to an assault on any of its 32 members.
"If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," he said. "We will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile."
The warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow.
"We stand here together in Poland today stronger than ever united in our common vision of a more balanced, more ready and more lethal alliance," Grynkewich also said.
European officials have accused Russia of waging a campaign of hybrid warfare involving sabotage, arson and cyberattacks, alongside increasingly provocative military activity near NATO territory.
I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA
Grynkewich's warning came amid heightened tensions between Russia and Western nations following a series of drone incursions and suspected sabotage operations that European countries have linked to Moscow. (Photo by Artur Widak/Anadolu via Getty Images)
In 2025, multiple Russian drones entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on Ukraine, prompting a response from Polish and allied aircraft.
NATO launched Operation Eastern Sentry to strengthen defenses along its eastern flank.
Romania has also reported Russian drone incursions , while Estonia has accused Russian military aircraft of violating its airspace.
Grynkewich's remarks had followed a tense weekend between Russia and Ukraine, with Moscow launching fresh strikes against Ukrainian energy infrastructure despite diplomatic efforts to reduce hostilities.
President Donald Trump had announced that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to the U.S. and global markets.
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad, its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania. ( Photo by Contributor/Getty Images)
The reported agreement included a waiver of certain U.S. sanctions on Russian energy exports.
Zelenskyy went on to accuse Russia of continuing attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities, casting doubt on prospects for a broader ceasefire.
The tensions have also been accompanied by recent nuclear warnings from Moscow.
On Sept. 30, Russia warned NATO that it could use nuclear weapons if the alliance attempted to isolate Kaliningrad , its heavily militarized Baltic Sea exclave between Poland and Lithuania.
In a diplomatic note obtained by Reuters , Moscow accused NATO of pursuing a "dangerous and reckless course" that carried "high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict."
According to the note, Russia warned it could use its full military arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend Kaliningrad and raised the possibility of strikes against decision-making centers in NATO countries at the outset of a conflict.
RUSSIA'S NEIGHBOR REVEALS PERSONAL APPEALS TO TRUMP AS US WEIGHS NATO TROOP PULLBACK IN EUROPE
The Hague, Netherlands - In photos, NATO leaders participate in the summit in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 25, 2025. NATO countries pledged to increase their defense spending to 5% of GDP by 2035, as demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump. The summit's final declaration states that countries will invest "at least 3.5%" of their GDP annually in military capabilities and an additional 1.5% in protecting critical infrastructure. (Handout / Latin America News Agency via Reuters Connect)
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte rejected the threats, emphasizing the alliance's defensive mission and calling on Moscow to end its war in Ukraine.
"Putin knows that he can never win from NATO," Rutte said during a Sept. 30 appearance at the Euronews Defence and Space Summit .
Putin has also maintained that Russia has no plans to attack European countries and wants peaceful coexistence with its neighbors.
Grynkewich did not mention Russia by name during his Warsaw address, but his warning appeared directed at Moscow and with NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept also identifying Russia as the most significant and direct threat to allied security.
"My theory of victory is simple: we will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent enemy advance," Grynkewich said on Monday.
"And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational warfighting system that is arrayed against us."
Grynkewich said NATO was already putting the strategy into action through military exercises, enhanced military readiness and investments in new capabilities.
SHE GREW UP UNDER SOVIET RULE. NOW EU'S TOP DIPLOMAT WARNS EUROPE AGAINST GIVING RUSSIA WHAT IT WANTS
NATO Secretary Gen. Mark Rutte attempts to assure President Donald Trump on Wednesday in a news conference that allies are increasing their financial commitments so Europe's defense is not all on the U.S. taxpayers. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
"If attacked, we are ready to fight tonight, but we are not complacent," he said.
The general made clear that NATO's response would not necessarily be limited to enemy troops directly involved in an assault, but could extend to the broader military infrastructure enabling the attack.
Meanwhile, Trump has pressed European allies to increase defense spending and has questioned whether countries that fail to meet their obligations should expect U.S. protection.
Grynkewich sought to downplay concerns about Washington's commitment, recalling Trump's positive remarks about the alliance during the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, Netherlands.
"I was in the room and I felt the love," Grynkewich said of the 2025 event.
"What I want to do is assure the one billion citizens of our alliance that we've got this. We know what we need to do. We know how we would do it," he added.
He also indicated a willingness to discuss suspected hybrid attacks more openly if individual NATO governments wanted him to address their concerns.
"If a nation wants me to, I'm happy to talk about it," he said.

articles.title_orig: California beaches, homes slammed by waves from Tropical Storm Rachel
articles.title_zh: California beaches, homes slammed by waves from Tropical Storm Rachel
articles.content_orig:
By LAUREN ACTON-TAYLOR, US NEWS REPORTER
Published: 21:37 EDT, 11 October 2026 | Updated: 12:07 EDT, 12 October 2026
A powerful storm in California has battered waterfront property as monster waves whipped up by Tropical Storm Rachel tore away nearly 30 feet of a boardwalk.
A century-old boardwalk in Long Beach was seen being ripped apart by blistering winds and towering waves as pricey homes risk collapsing into the waters.
On Saturday evening, officials taped off the boardwalk with 'No Trespassing' signs as eight homes were red-tagged as unsafe to enter on the city's Peninsula, Mayor Rex Richardson said.
A ninth home was left yellow-tagged, allowing the home occupants access to grab their belongings but not stay in the property.
The tags, however, are not necessarily permanent. A red tag can be downgraded to yellow once repairs are made and inspectors approve the property, with inspections set to continue twice daily.
Officials are continuing to assess the threat and determine whether evacuation orders will be necessary as another round of severe weather looms.
Chilling footage on Friday night showed towering swells crashing against a home in the 6500 block of Seaside Walk, reaching its second-story windows as sections of the building and broken pieces of boardwalk drifted into the ocean.
Other images showed floodwaters engulfing nearby side streets and patios, pouring into homes and properties left badly damaged.
A century-old boardwalk in Long Beach was seen being ripped apart by blistering winds and towering waves as pricey homes risk collapsing into the waters
On Saturday evening, officials taped off the boardwalk with 'No Trespassing' signs as eight homes were red-tagged as unsafe to enter on the city's Peninsula
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning on Friday afternoon for Los Angeles County beaches until 3pm on Sunday, as forecasters expected waves reaching four to seven feet
More recent video saw a structure being pulled off the ground, with two people attempting to claw it onto the ground until one of them was lifted from the floor, the California Post reported.
'It is not normal that we see this type of activity,' Mayor Richardson said on Saturday.
'Just in this season, this marks the third hurricane in just six weeks. We saw Hurricane Marie over Labor Day, which was followed soon by Hurricane Polo, and now Rachel is bringing with it more high tides, more surf, erosion that continues to cause damage to properties and damage along our coastline.'
'This is easily the most damage I have seen over the past couple of weeks,' said KTLA's Rich Prickett, whose crew captured the destruction from a helicopter overhead.
'Now the entire boardwalk is just starting to shred away, and now some of these homes are being impacted even more severely,' he added.
'As you’re seeing this house right here that’s starting to crumble as that erosion just continues underneath the house.'
The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning on Friday afternoon for Los Angeles County beaches until 3pm on Sunday, as forecasters expected waves reaching four to seven feet.
'It’s really heartbreaking to see how much has been affected with the surf and the high tides and everything. I mean, people are losing their houses,' Stacey Sniezak, Long Beach neighbor, told ABC 7 .
High tides over seven feet are expected in the mornings, as forecasters expect conditions may deteriorate on Sunday from strong winds, rain and elevated ocean water levels
Rain is expected to spread on Saturday night into Sunday morning, with showers possibly continuing through Tuesday night
Local officials distributed 7,600 sandbags in hopes of helping residents protect their properties

Sniezak said the damage to her home, where she has lived for 45 years, has left her devastated.
'It’s just impossible to fix at this point, and I don’t know how they’re going to do that,' she added.
Richardson announced all vehicle access to the Peninsula had been closed off for residents only, and added: 'We're encouraging everyone else to avoid the Peninsula all weekend, so that our city crews can have access and best perform this critical work.'
The Weather Service warned that coastal flooding could lead to damaged beach roads and structures, as well as significant beach erosion.
High tides over seven feet are expected in the mornings, as forecasters expect conditions may deteriorate on Sunday from strong winds, rain and elevated ocean water levels.
The Weather Service urged residents and visitors to stay off beaches, coastal walkways and vulnerable roads and structures. Motorists were warned not to drive around barricades or through floodwaters.
Rain is expected to spread on Saturday night into Sunday morning, with showers possibly continuing through Tuesday night.
Local officials distributed 7,600 sandbags in hopes of helping residents protect their properties.
'We’re looking at an unprecedented high tide, potentially 7.8 to 8 feet, which is significant for this area,' Long Beach Fire Department Assistant Chief Jake Heflin said.
'We’re not just talking about the peninsula, we’re not talking just about Naples, we’re talking about the potential for a citywide impact.'
