articles.title_orig: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
articles.title_zh: Boardroom feud tests trusted Indian business empire
articles.content_orig:
Before dawn breaks over Mumbai, Mansi Kadam begins preparing vada pav, a savoury snack synonymous with the western Indian city, for the day's customers. One ingredient is non-negotiable: Tata salt.
When asked whether she would ever consider switching brands, her reply is a reminder of an old Hindi ad jingle, "If it's salt, it has to be Tata."
She knows little about the developments unfolding in the boardroom of the Tata group, one of India's oldest and most influential business empires that makes everything from salt to software.
But her instinctive loyalty points to a question confronting the group: Can one of India's most trusted brands remain insulated from a public battle over power, governance and control?
A recent public disagreement between the board of Tata Sons, the holding company of the Tata group and Tata Trusts, its principal shareholder, has put a spotlight on the conglomerate.
At the centre of the dispute are two issues - the proposed public listing of Tata Sons and the reappointment of chairman N Chandrasekaran . Most of the Tata Sons board, including its biggest minority shareholder SP Group, supported the decisions.
But Noel Tata, chairman of majority shareholder Tata Trusts, has opposed both resolutions. He maintains that a public listing would dilute the group's philanthropic ethos and is likely to get both decisions overturned at its annual general meeting.
"When we say this is a governance crisis, it's a misalignment of interests between the board [of Tata Sons] and the shareholders [Tata Trusts]," Shriram Subramanian, head of independent corporate governance firm InGovern Research, told the BBC.
While he does not expect the brand's image to be affected immediately, he flags concerns over the leadership's ability to navigate the challenges.
Disagreements within the Tata Group have been simmering since the death of former chairman Ratan Tata - Noel Tata's half-brother who designated him successor after his death - in 2024. For many Indians, Ratan Tata's philanthropy and leadership had become inseparable from the brand. His death triggered widespread mourning and experts say it left a leadership void in the group's image with the public.
The Tata group has topped India's most valuable brand list by valuation consultancy Brand Finance since 2018, according to the group's website.
Tata Sons, the business entity, is described by the group as the "fastener keeping the many disparate elements of the whole together".
Tata Trusts, which represents seven philanthropic trusts that own the majority stake in the group, is widely regarded as its moral compass, guiding the businesses on social impact and philanthropy.
For many Indians, both the entities together make up what most companies cannot buy - trust.
Now with these entities in rival corners, that is coming under strain.
"Once upon a time, there was a unified audience which said the Tatas are good people with good governance. Today, the opinion is divided," said Harish Bijoor, business and brand strategy consultant.
While most consumers appear unfazed, the dispute has polarised other stakeholders including business partners, investors and employees. Some view it as corporate power politics, others as a genuine governance debate, but few agree on which side is right, Bijoor said.
"This conflict has brought the Tatas into conversations everywhere, which is not good as they have always liked to be out of it," he says.
The group has been traditionally preferred being low profile about philanthropy and conflict resolution.
The Tata group did not respond to BBC's email with detailed questions.
Founded by Jamsetji Tata in 1868, the Tata group expanded under JRD Tata who transformed it into a professionally managed conglomerate. Ratan Tata drove its global ambitions through acquisitions.
Tata group, which has a combined market value of more than $260bn (£195.6bn) and employs hundreds of thousands of people in more than 100 countries, is not new to controversies.
The conglomerate has faced protests over industrial projects, scrutiny of its Indian telecom business during a spectrum allocation controversy, a high-profile dispute with Japan's Docomo and, more recently, questions over Air India's performance .
Some of its business decisions have also drawn attention, particularly Tata Steel's troubled Corus acquisition, though other overseas bets such as Tetley and Jaguar Land Rover were successful and helped expand the group's global footprint.
Its biggest controversy was in 2016 when the Tata Sons board abruptly removed Cyrus Mistry as chairman and brought back Ratan Tata as interim head. Mistry, heir to the SP Group, was chosen by a team led by Ratan Tata himself. It led to a long battle which ended in 2021 with the Supreme Court ruling in the Tatas' favour.
Last month, journalist Sucheta Dalal wrote in her column for Moneylife magazine that the Tata group has "weathered serious governance storms" and enjoys "special privileges available to no other business group [referring to a tax exemption granted to Tata Trusts for holding shares in Tata Sons]" because of a reputation built over decades.
In an email interview, Morgen Witzel, a fellow at Exeter Centre of Leadership who wrote a book on the brand in 2010, cited several examples on the group's connection with people.
At Jamshedpur in Jharkhand state, where the group set up India's first integrated steel plant and an industrial city, it provides healthcare and education to people in hundreds of villages. Watchmaker Titan supports employees who want to leave and start their own businesses. Tata Motors at Pune has supported thousands of female entrepreneurs, he points out.
"It is the concatenation of all of these things that builds trust because people see that, by and large, Tata is there to serve their needs rather than just take their money," Witzel said.
But while the group has weathered other storms, this time, the divide is within.
The boardroom tussle has increasingly spilled into the public domain, with Tata Sons and Trusts clashing through legal notices and conflicting statements.
Venu Srinivasan, vice-chairman of Tata Trusts and a nominee director on Tata Sons' board, has sought a probe into alleged governance lapses at some trusts. The trusts deny the lapses.
Noel Tata has made two proposals to avoid listing the company.
First, that the Tata Sons board buy back a portion of SP Group's minority stake as a "fair and equitable solution" to the latter's demand to monetise their stake. Secondly, restructure Tata Sons by merging with itself two businesses which would change the way it is classified by India's central bank,  helping the group potentially avoid a listing.
It is not clear whether he can pull this off, given that unlike Rata Tata, he had not consolidated power yet.
"Ratan Tata's larger-than-life image is, to some extent, the reason behind the current conflict. Everyone was deferential towards him and his successor was known only after his death through his will," says Subramanian.
Had Ratan Tata overseen the succession himself, the transition would have been smoother, he says.
Brand expert Bijoor calls for the Tata group to put together a "white paper" on how the conflict plays out in the end. "They stood for transparency, and they must never shed that."
How the influential group manages these tensions may offer a glimpse into its future. The outcome will be watched closely across corporate India, where Tata's governance and business practices have long been regarded as a benchmark.

articles.title_orig: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.title_zh: World’s tiniest flowering plant could feed deep space astronauts
articles.content_orig:
Duckweed on end of pencil. (University of Nottingham via SWNS)
The world’s smallest flowering plant would be an “ideal” food crop for future space missions , according to new research.
Duckweeds measure just a few millimeters across, but scientists say they could feed astronauts exploring deep space — as well as providing a potential source of food and protein on Earth.
Researchers at the University of Nottingham conducted gene expression analysis and cutting-edge microscopy on duckweeds.
Their findings, published in the journal Current Biology , show that they retain the same basic building blocks found in the shoots of larger plants.
But those structures have been “dramatically compressed” and fused together.
(Photo by Samiran Biswas via Pexels)
Study leader Anthony Bishopp says miniaturization is a “remarkable phenomenon” found throughout the natural world, from tiny animals to miniature plants.
He said: “Duckweeds are extraordinary flowering plants that can measure just a few millimeters across, yet their relatives include some of the largest herbaceous plants.
“We were interested to find out how a complete plant body plan can be packed into such a tiny space.
“While miniaturization in animals is often associated with the loss of organs or body structures, we have revealed that duckweeds have taken a different route.
“What surprised us is that, when we looked closely, the basic organization of the shoot was still there.
“Rather than throwing away parts of the blueprint, duckweed appears to have compressed and fused its components into an incredibly compact plant.
(Photo by Petr Ganaj via Pexels)
“That gives us a new way of thinking about how plants can evolve to become so small.”
Bishopp said duckweed research is advancing rapidly, driven by growing interest in the tiny plants as a potential source of food and novel protein on Earth, as well as a possible crop for future space missions.
He added: “Unlike most of the crops we grow today, which have been shaped by thousands of years of domestication and selective breeding, the potential of duckweed remains largely unexplored.
“Even the basic architecture of the duckweed plant has remained something of a mystery.
“Understanding how its body is organized provides an essential framework for understanding how duckweed grows, develops and functions — and ultimately how its potential might be improved.”
Study co-author Alex Ware said: “Duckweeds are astonishingly small, so it is tempting to think of them as either primitive plants or simply as having lost parts, but this is not the case.”
Ware added: “Our research adds to growing evidence from across the research community about this plant and will help efforts to turn them into a future crop.”

articles.title_orig: Man dies after falling off roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, police and witnesses say
articles.title_zh: Man dies after falling off roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, police and witnesses say
articles.content_orig:
A man has died at Six Flags Over Georgia, police said, with witnesses telling CNN affiliate WXIA they watched the man fall off a roller coaster.
Several others were injured, Cobb County police said.
One witness told WXIA the falling man was captured on his souvenir picture taken while on the Goliath ride.
The 210-second ride reaches a top speed of 70 mph and an elevation of 200 feet, according to the Six Flags website .
Six Flags Over Georgia addressed the incident in a statement, saying: “We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest’s family, friends, and loved ones.”
Similar attractions at “sister” parks across the country have been temporarily closed “out of an abundance of caution,” a park spokesperson said Monday evening.
The Georgia theme park was already scheduled to be closed Tuesday, the spokesperson added.
Other riders were being evacuated from the roller coaster, aerial video from WXIA showed.
The theme park is about 10 miles west of downtown Atlanta.
The death comes nearly two weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in California announced it will permanently close its world-famous ride X2, following a CNN investigation that exposed a long history of life-altering injuries and deaths linked to the roller coaster.
Six Flags to close world-famous roller coaster after CNN investigation exposed years of injuries and deaths
Six Flags Magic Mountain President Brian Oerding wrote in a blog post that while the X2 roller coaster has “consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it’s the right thing to do.”
He added, “Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously.”
Allegations that the Southern California thrill ride injured riders date back more than a decade, but had been largely kept under wraps until CNN’s investigation this summer revealed more than a dozen reports of serious injuries and hospitalizations associated with the ride, including at least two deaths. Most recently, two women ended up in the same Santa Clarita emergency room with brain injuries after riding X2 just six days apart in July.
This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title_orig: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
articles.title_zh: CNBC's The China Connection newsletter: How a gold-buying spree helps the yuan go global
articles.content_orig:
Hi, this is Evelyn, writing to you from Beijing. Welcome to the latest edition of The China Connection — a snapshot of what I'm seeing and hearing from local businesses.
Buying gold every month for nearly two years is just part of China's plan to narrow a gap with the U.S. on holdings of the precious metal. What does that do to the yuan?
China's decades-long push for yuan internationalization is getting a lift from the buildout of Hong Kong as a gold trading center — denominated in the Chinese currency.
"As those trading volumes grow, there would be a growing volume of the physical gold trade that is denominated in RMB and not linked in USD," said Charles Chang, managing director and Greater China country lead for corporate ratings at S&P Global Ratings.
The Chinese yuan, also known as the renminbi, accounts for a fraction of international transactions in a global financial system dominated by the U.S. dollar. Analysts I spoke with don't expect major changes to that dynamic anytime soon, but Beijing's gold purchases and Hong Kong trading platform are just the latest steps toward supporting greater use of the yuan globally.
"The challenge with internationalizing the RMB it's somewhat more challenging to find places where you can use the RMB," Chang said. "In terms of gold particularly, if the RMB that the buyer receives can be converted to gold, then it gives more channels for the spending to be done."
Hong Kong, home to one of the world's largest stock exchanges, last month confirmed its efforts to develop a yuan-denominated gold market .
In a major move last year, the special administrative region of China linked its gold vault with one in Shanghai , allowing physical gold delivery to international institutions in Hong Kong denominated in yuan.
Over the next three years, Hong Kong plans to expand the capacity of its Shanghai-linked gold vault from 150 tonnes to over 2,000 tonnes , S&P's Chang pointed out.
That's nearly as large as all the gold reserves in China , he added. "If Hong Kong is able to complete this transaction, then it would become of the largest gold trading centers in the world."
The U.S. still has the largest gold reserves in the world at over 8,100 tonnes, according to World Gold Council figures for the second quarter. China held about one-third of that at over 2,300 tonnes.
"China's 23-month gold buying streak reinforces the credibility of the renminbi's internationalization drive," said Hao Zhou, head of research and chief economist at Guotai Junan International in Hong Kong.
"By steadily increasing gold reserves, Beijing is strengthening the long-term backing of its financial system and reducing reliance on dollar-denominated reserve assets," he said. "While gold alone will not determine the RMB's global role, it enhances confidence in the currency and supports broader efforts to expand its use in trade, investment and official reserves."
Gold accumulation by China and other countries' central banks will help reduce global reliance on U.S. Treasurys and U.S. dollar reserves, said Xia Yingying, head of the precious metals and new energy research group, at Hangzhou-based Nanhua Futures. That's according to a CNBC translation of the Chinese.
"This will suppress the U.S. dollar's premium from being a core reserve currency, and raise the risk premium associated with the dollar regarding credit, fiscal policy and sanctions," Xia said. "In the medium to-long-term it will gradually weaken the U.S. dollar's monopolistic position in the global reserve system."
China's growing gold purchases, however, also come as U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday named gold-standard supporter Judy Shelton as a senior advisor focused on China .
The Asian economy's rise as a manufacturing powerhouse benefited from the U.S. decision to abandon the gold standard more than 50 years ago. "With the delinking of the dollar and gold, and the consequent rise in the oil price, western manufacturing became less economic, and capital went to Asia in search of cheap labor and overall lower costs," wrote the central bank research group OMFIF in 2021.
While China is the largest consumer and producer of gold, it is just one of many developing economies that has expanded its reserves since 2022, according to S&P. The World Gold Council showed Poland has increased its gold reserves by more tonnes than China.
The trend goes beyond financial transactions. Like with rare earths, Beijing's gold ambitions start with control of some of the product.
China has acquired major gold mines across Latin America, Africa and Asia, according to S&P Global Ratings.
"China's plans for gold and its activities in gold are comprehensive and long lasting. These trends are going to be in place for a number of years," Chang said.
"The comprehensive nature of this," he said, "is something that markets often miss."
DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say
China's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion), double its earlier target, with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. AI startup Manus raises $500 million from IDG Capital and others, indicating investors aren't deterred by Beijing's unprecedented order to block Meta's short-lived $2 billion acquisition.
China and Europe agree to halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports
European trade commissioner Maroš Sefčovič said Friday that China has agreed to halve its exports of hybrid cars to the bloc. China's auto market is on track for its worst year since 2021, with sales down by more than 20% over roughly the first three quarters of the year, according to China Passenger Car Association data as of Sept. 27.
After a yearslong slump, China's real estate market may be set for a turnaround
Residential real estate prices may hit a bottom in the third quarter of 2028 , S&P Global Ratings said. It added that prices in China's largest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, will likely recover as soon as next year.

articles.title_orig: AM Broadcasters in Chile Face a Dilemma
articles.title_zh: AM Broadcasters in Chile Face a Dilemma
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › Columns and Views › Guest Commentaries
The author is a broadcaster and director of Radio Romance in Santiago, Chile.
AM radio is facing a crisis that can no longer be explained simply by declining audiences. The deeper problem is technological, economic and regulatory.
Without clear pathways to evolve, many stations risk disappearing. I am writing here about stations in Chile, but the discussion will have resonance anywhere AM radio is used.
For decades, AM radio was one of Chile’s most important communications platforms. It informed communities during earthquakes, accompanied listeners through the night, carried sports, news, music and conversation, and reached places other media could not.
Today, however, AM broadcasters are competing in a radically different ecosystem with technology that has lost much of its commercial appeal and, in many places, its listening convenience.
What should an AM station do in order to survive? The answer seems obvious: migrate.
Migration does not necessarily mean abandoning radio or erasing its history. It means allowing broadcasters to test new technologies, explore other bands, integrate effectively with digital platforms and find sustainable models that can preserve their role.
The alternative is much harsher: disappearance.
Chile should address this as a communications policy issue, not merely as a series of isolated problems affecting individual stations. When a broadcaster faces economic distress, loses access to a transmission facility or is forced to suspend operations temporarily, public policy should at least ask what tools exist to help a legitimate broadcaster adapt.
Today, Radio Romance is off the air on its terrestrial signal. We maintain only a minimal digital presence, with a basic music stream, so that Radio Romance does not disappear completely.
But this stream does not replace the radio station we built, nor does our current website reflect the full reality of what Radio Romance was and what we want to rebuild.
For a broadcaster, silence on the dial is extraordinarily painful.
Radio Romance has a history, an identity, an audience, thousands of hours of content and, above all, the determination to continue. What we do not have today is a technological bridge that would allow us to move from an AM model that has become increasingly difficult to sustain toward a viable future for broadcasting.
Other communications technologies have gone through managed transitions. Television moved from analog to digital. Telecommunications networks evolved. Mobile technology changed repeatedly. The answer to technological obsolescence has rarely been simply to let operators disappear.
Radio deserves the same discussion.
Chile has seen experimental broadcasting experiences involving AM operators and the lower FM band. If such experiments exist, it is reasonable to ask what criteria govern access, how another broadcaster may apply and what mechanism allows a traditional AM station to present a serious technology-transition project.
This is not about giving frequencies away.
It is not about eliminating technical requirements or ignoring the state’s legitimate role in managing scarce spectrum.
It is about something more basic: making the rules known and giving broadcasters an opportunity to be assessed under them.
We have asked the regulator for an opportunity to present and evaluate experimental alternatives that could offer a different technological path.
Our experience is bigger than the future of one station.
It reflects the situation of an industry that needs answers.
An AM broadcaster should not have to choose only between remaining indefinitely on an increasingly difficult-to-finance platform or disappearing.
There should be a third option: evolve.
Broadcasting also has a characteristic that is easy to overlook when viewed only through financial metrics: when a media outlet disappears, a voice disappears with it. A company may close, but when that company is a media outlet, an editorial, cultural and social window closes too.
That is why the future of AM is also a question of media pluralism. We do not need to preserve technologies artificially out of nostalgia. Nostalgia is not public policy. But technological change should not eliminate media outlets that still have experience, audiences, content and a willingness to continue simply because no bridge was built to the next technological environment.
That bridge deserves serious discussion.
Further, the disappearance of AM radio has a human dimension that can hardly be measured in numbers.
For decades, every station was surrounded by an entire ecosystem of technicians, operators, engineers, broadcasters, journalists, producers and collaborators who made it possible for a human voice to travel hundreds of miles.
Many devoted 30 or 40 years of their lives to this profession. Today, when an AM station ceases operations, they do not simply lose a job. They discover that the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime have fewer and fewer places where they can still be put to use. Behind every transmitter that goes silent are professionals, collaborators, and families confronting the gradual disappearance of the working world to which they once belonged.
On the other side of the receiver, something equally painful is happening.
Thousands of adults and older listeners grew up with these stations. For decades, they listened in their homes, cars, workshops and across the countryside. For them, radio was never merely a means of communication. It was companionship, routine, familiarity, and memory.
Saying that these audiences can simply move to the internet does not solve the problem. Many older adults are unfamiliar with apps and digital platforms; others, even when they know how to use them, cannot find the voices and programs that became part of their lives.
There is also a profoundly symbolic image: enormous antennas and transmitting facilities standing motionless in fields. Places once alive with technicians at work, transmitters operating day and night, and signals traveling across vast territories are now falling silent, often with little realistic possibility of ever being used again.
It is the gradual end of an entire ecosystem: people, professions, trades, listeners, memories, antennas and transmitters.
When an AM radio station goes off the air, the silence is not confined to the dial. It also remains with those who devoted their lives to making that radio possible — and with those who spent a lifetime in its company.
The solution may involve experimental technologies, new spectrum arrangements, digital broadcasting, hybrid radio and online distribution, and regulatory mechanisms that allow existing broadcasters to submit credible transition projects.
The important first step is to acknowledge the problem.
For much of AM radio, time is no longer measured in decades.
It may be measured in years — and for some operators, perhaps months. The question Chile should be asking is simple: Do we want to manage the disappearance of AM radio, or manage its transformation?
Those of us who have spent our lives in broadcasting are not asking for privileges.
We are not asking anyone to give us a frequency. We are asking for the opportunity to transform. Because when technology changes, there are ultimately two paths: migrate or die.

articles.title_orig: New report shows US chip industry’s reliance on China
articles.title_zh: New report shows US chip industry’s reliance on China
articles.content_orig:
US chip production relies on ‘vulnerable inputs hidden deep in upstream global supply chains’, SIA says
China accounts for about 5 per cent of the equipment and materials directly supplied to the US chip industry when measured by country of manufacture, but its grip on certain rare earths needed for chipmaking is over 90 per cent, according to the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA).
While 95 per cent of the nearly US$27 billion annual spending by American chipmakers on manufacturing equipment and materials was sourced from companies headquartered in the US, Europe, and Japan, that figure dropped to 68 per cent when the value is counted by country of origin, according to SIA.
Suppliers “often rely on production chains outside their country of domicile”, the SIA said in a report published on Friday.

If you’re eager to get your hands on the highly anticipated iPhone Duo , the first foldable iPhone, here’s how to get a head start on ordering. Apple has opened a staging page for preorders on apple.com , where you can get ready to place a preorder for the viral phone.
Head over to Apple’s online storefront, and you’ll find that a new iPhone Duo configurator is now live. On that page, save your preferred phone color, storage, mobile carrier and payment method. Saving these details in advance ensures you can complete your purchase immediately when preorders open at 5 a.m. PT on Friday.
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo , one of its first new products under the helm of new CEO John Ternus, during its Surprise and Shine event in Cupertino, California, on Friday. It’s the first foldable from Apple, although merely the latest in a wave of new bendy phones to hit the market.
The iPhone Duo opens to reveal a 7.6-inch display and folds down to a pocketable passport size. The shifting shape supports split-screen multitasking and Apple Pencil, and brings a host of new features and animations to Apple iOS 27 .
Pricing starts at $1,999 for the 512GB model and tops out at $3,199 for the 2TB version — before carrier subsidies — making the iPhone Duo the most expensive iPhone ever released. Price aside, observers expect demand among early adopters to be high, so prepping your order now is a smart idea.
Not quite sure that the new iPhone Duo is the right phone for you? I’m also on the fence. Check out CNET’s coverage leading up to the launch of the new foldable and iOS 27 , as well as the more conventionally shaped iPhone 18 Pro , so you can make an informed decision.

EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE) - Fall break is underway for some area schools, and the Children’s Museum of Evansville is creating new ways for students to enjoy their time off while continuing to learn.
The museum is debuting its “Travel the World Week” activity, featuring Australia.
From constructing models of the Sydney Harbour Bridge to creating art inspired by Australia’s unique landscape, museum staff say there are plenty of activities planned for children.
“We have more than three stories of interactive exhibits and experiences for families to explore and its just important for families to be able to learn outside of school and during these breaks that they’re actively not in a school setting,” said Hannah Dupuy-McClure with the Children’s Museum of Evansville.
Organizers say they hope the event gives students an opportunity to recognize that learning can exist well beyond the classroom.

articles.title_orig: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
articles.title_zh: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
articles.content_orig:
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption
Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.
An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social .
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."
The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.
The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.
The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.
The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."
Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.
"The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."
The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.
It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.

articles.title_orig: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.title_zh: World-famous science educator Bill Nye believes in Titans: ‘You're going to change the world’
articles.content_orig:
When the first notes of the “Bill Nye the Science Guy” theme song began echoing through the Titan Student Union Portola Pavilion, students didn’t miss a beat. They sang along to the popular chorus — “Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill, Bill” — as the world-famous scientist and educator took the stage for the “Beyond the Conversation” series at Cal State Fullerton.
Hosted by Associated Students Inc., the signature series invites notable speakers to campus to share their stories and spark dialogue among students. Bill Nye, who spoke to the Titan community on Oct. 7, joins a star-studded lineup of previous “Beyond the Conversation” speakers, including Olympic swimmer Michael Phelps , Oscar winner Ke Huy Quan , and Emmy and Grammy Award-winning actress Cynthia Erivo .
As the co-creator and host of the Emmy Award-winning ’90s television series “Bill Nye the Science Guy,” Nye has emerged not only as an entertaining educator but also as an influential advocate for science and facts in an era of misinformation.
His lifelong commitment to advocacy has earned him various honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, inclusion in the Time 100 Health list, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards.
Nye has made science and engineering education entertaining and accessible for generations of viewers. He shared his story with Cal State Fullerton students and imparted a few pieces of advice and encouragement to help them on their academic journey.
Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.  — Bill Nye
“You guys are going to graduate from Cal State Fullerton with this degree, and it will be worth more the day after you graduate than the day you graduate. I guarantee you,” Nye said.
“Getting a college education gives you a way of looking at the world that is essentially priceless. You are going to go out there and dare I say it, change the world.”
With the rapid expansion of social media and artificial intelligence, Nye acknowledged that students have access to a wealth of information about science, the environment and sustainability. He said the key to consuming and identifying reliable information is critical thinking.
As a scientist who has spent his career asking questions and investigating the wonders of the world, Nye said critical thinking isn’t about questioning everything and assuming everything is wrong. It’s about evaluating evidence before deciding if a claim is true.
“What we want everybody to embrace is what is nowadays called critical thinking. It used to be called logic or logical reasoning, but we want everybody to be in the habit of evaluating evidence,” Nye explained.
For students who are preparing to launch their careers, Nye said it’s important to lead with passion and curiosity and to take that first step.
“My advice is to just get started. You don’t know where it’s going to lead, but find something you want to do or something that you wouldn’t mind doing, and get started,” Nye said.
“The thing that goes wrong is when you have so many things to do, you just can’t get going. Just get started. You’re going to change the world.”
Nye was interviewed by Nathan Hoang, a fourth-year business administration student and student programmer for ASI’s student programs and engagement team.
“Events like ‘Beyond the Conversation’ inspire students to see themselves in these figures and empower them to believe maybe they can one day be on that stage as well,” Hoang said. “What stood out to me about Bill’s interview was how he kept the conversation fun, but still didn’t shy away from pointing out our responsibilities as young adults and the potential we have to shape the future.”

articles.title_zh: Person dies at Six Flags Over Georgia; video shows Goliath ride being evacuated in Austell
articles.content_orig:
AUSTELL, Ga. -- One person died and several others were injured in an "incident involving a roller coaster" at a Six Flags amusement park in Georgia, authorities said.
The incident occurred at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County shortly before 4 p.m. Monday, according to police.
"Officers assigned to the park, along with uniformed patrol officers, responded to the scene," the Cobb County Police Department said in a statement. "Detectives with our Major Crimes Unit are responding to investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident."
Police did not release any further details on the incident.
Riders on the amusement park's Goliath roller coaster were seen being evacuated off the ride on Monday.
A Six Flags spokesperson said that the "park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation."
"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," the spokesperson said in a statement. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends, and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected."
The spokesperson added that they will not be releasing additional information at this time "out of respect for the family's privacy."
Six Flags Over Georgia is located in Austell, west of Atlanta.
This is a breaking story; check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: China’s carmakers boost exports amid EU limits on hybrid vehicle imports
articles.title_zh: China’s carmakers boost exports amid EU limits on hybrid vehicle imports
articles.content_orig:
China’s passenger car exports rose 64% in September from September 2025, an industry association reported on Monday. Chinese automakers are increasingly focusing on exports amid sluggish domestic sales. In September, China exported about 919,000 passenger vehicles, driven by demand for plug-in hybrids and electric vehicles.
In the first nine months of 2026, China exported more than 7.1 million passenger cars, up more than 70% from the previous year. In contrast, domestic sales fell 27% year-on-year in September to over 1.6 million units, driven by weakened consumer confidence and reduced government subsidies.
Despite being the world’s largest vehicle exporter, China faces scepticism from trade partners concerned about its impact on local industries. The European Union is capping imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 per year.
Chinese car sales grow in regions including Europe
In recent months, Chinese automakers have targeted growth in international markets, including Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Canada is also opening up to Chinese EV exports under a new tariff agreement. Analysts like Stephen Chan from S&P Global Ratings note that the industry is relying more on overseas sales to offset weaknesses in the domestic market. Consultancy AlixPartners predicts that Chinese automakers may export nearly 10 million vehicles globally by 2026. In Europe, they compete effectively by offering lower production costs; for example, a Chinese EV costs about $20,000 to produce, compared with around $31,000 for a European counterpart.
EU to cap Chinese hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 annually
The EU has imposed higher tariffs on pure electric vehicles from China, prompting Chinese manufacturers to export more hybrid vehicles. A Deutsche Bank research note indicates that in August, Chinese automakers captured about 12% of Europe’s new car market, accounting for one in four hybrid sales.
To address concerns about trade imbalances, EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič announced an interim agreement that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the EU. This agreement establishes an annual import quota of 350,000 hybrid vehicles from China, including plug-in hybrids. Customs authorities across the 27-nation bloc will monitor these imports and halt shipments once the quota is reached, starting as early as December. This limit excludes cars made in Europe by Chinese companies.
Analysts warn that these protectionist measures may hinder Chinese automakers’ growth in Europe. Xiao Feng from CITIC CLSA noted that companies like BYD may struggle to export cars amid tariffs and political resistance. BYD’s executive vice president, Stella Li , acknowledged that geopolitics pose significant challenges to their expansion. To adapt, BYD is establishing production plants in Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, and Hungary.
More overseas production limits impact from trade curbs
Chinese automakers are expected to expand overseas production to minimise tariff exposure, according to Ming Lee of BofA Global Research. He noted that more production will be localised. Meanwhile, high tariffs have effectively barred Chinese electric vehicles (EVs) from the US market. A recent meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping produced no agreement on this issue, and experts suggest ongoing political uncertainty makes the US market a lower priority for Chinese automakers.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Deadly Houthi attacks keep Saudi airport closed as Trump considers U.S. strikes in Yemen
articles.content_orig:
Saudi Arabia has launched an investigation to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, including an attack on Riyadh airport that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300, two regional officials said Monday.
The officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the initial probe showed that Yemen's Houthis first fired multiple drones to pave the way for a mix of cruise and ballistic missiles to reach Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.
The Houthis possess ballistic missiles and advanced systems fitted with warheads that can change direction during flight and pose a challenge to Patriot interceptors and other defense systems used by the Saudis.
One of the officials said the investigation also aims to find out why air defense systems did not provide earlier warning of the attack in which the Houthi missiles and drones flew over 620 miles to reach Riyadh.
Delta Air Lines said Monday it is delaying plans for nonstop flights from Atlanta to Riyadh amid escalating attacks between Yemen's Houthi militants and Saudi Arabia.
"The safety and security of our customers and employees always come first and continue to guide our operational decisions," the company said in a statement. "We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation."
Delta announced last year its plans to operate nonstop flights to Riyadh three times a week on its Airbus A350-900 aircraft in October 2026. It said at the time that the new destination would help strengthen business and travel ties between the United States and Saudi Arabia.
The company said Monday the launch of Atlanta-Riyadh flights will take place in March 2027.
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday denied the U.K.'s allegations that Tehran was involved in last month's security incident at a British base used by American bombers.
In a statement posted to social media , the foreign ministry condemned what it said were "unfounded accusations by the United Kingdom against Iran."
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier Monday the security incident at RAF Fairford — which led to the arrests of seven men who were later released on bail — was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran" and "almost certainly" by the regime's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
In its response, Tehran said by using terms like "highly likely" and "almost" certain, the U.K. is "hiding behind vague language without presenting concrete evidence or proof."
Foreign ministers of NATO member countries on Monday issued a joint statement condemning "Iran's use of violent attacks, including the acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners."
The statement said the countries recognize the U.K.'s assertion that last month's security incident at RAF Fairford , a U.S.-run air base in Britain, was likely coordinated by Iran.
"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," the joint statement said. " Anyone who conducts hostile activities on behalf of Iran, or any other state, should know that we will take action to identify, investigate, disrupt, and prosecute these acts."
In a separate statement, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said he welcomes the statement issued by allies and partners, echoing their denouncement of "Iran's involvement in violence and threats on Allied territory."
"NATO will continue to do its part to safeguard the security of our one billion people across the Alliance," Rutte said.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed an attack targeting Riyadh's international airport on Monday, after a Saudi-led coalition said it had shot down a missile over the capital.
"Our armed forces were able to target (King) Khalid International Airport in the Saudi enemy's capital Riyadh this evening with a ballistic missile and the hit was precise," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said . He said the group also targeted the Khamis Mushait base in the kingdom's south with a drone.
Saree also warned against "the consequences of operating flights toward Saudi airports, as they are not safe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the sacred areas in Mecca al-Mukarramah and Medina al-Munawwarah."
It's unclear whether there were any injuries.
Several powerful explosions rattled the Saudi capital Riyadh on Monday night, just moments after a text message sent to residents' mobile phones warned of an aerial threat.
"The area is under a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm, stay indoors or in a safe place away from windows and doors," read the message.
Around the same time, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its forces intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Iran-backed group at the capital.
"Interception and destruction of a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," Major General Turki al-Malki, a spokesperson for the coalition, wrote in a post on X.
U.K. Foreign Minister Ed Miliband announced sanctions against two Iranian nationals on Monday, "for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," he said in a statement .
"We will not tolerate threats on British soil," said Miliband, who earlier had released a joint statement alongside his counterparts in the U.S., Australia, Canada and 23 other countries, which condemned hostile activities by Iran on foreign soil.
Their statements followed a security incident at the RAF Fairford air base in southern England, which U.K. government leaders and others have attributed to Iran. Iran denied its involvement Monday in comments released by state media.
The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said on Monday that American citizens had been detained for filming recent events in Saudi Arabia, which has suffered a string of deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
The embassy said "American citizens have been detained for taking photos of recent events," without specifying how many were arrested or whether they had been released. It noted that Saudi authorities have warned that "filming, publishing, or sharing information related to counter missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."
Several foreign residents in Riyadh have told AFP that acquaintances were detained for filming recent events and sharing the footage on social media.
Iran on Monday denied any involvement in a security incident at England's RAF Fairford air base, which the U.S. previously used to deploy long-range bombers during the war.
"The Iranian ambassador in London, Ali Moussavi, has again categorically rejected the accusations concerning Tehran's role in the incident at the Fairford military base," the Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, adding that he "called on the British government to present evidence supporting its allegations if it possesses any."
That statement followed earlier remarks from British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who said the incident was "almost certainly directed" by Iran's Revolutionary Guard.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Monday to have struck three supertankers in the Strait of Hormuz over the last two days.
The IRGC Navy said in its most recent attack on a ship, Monday, "a third non-compliant super-tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire."
It said the tanker had switched off the system that broadcasts a vessel's location in an effort to evade Iranian restrictions on navigating the strait without permission and "disregarded warnings from the IRGC Navy."

articles.title_zh: ‘There Are No Words’: Dozens Killed in Airstrikes Near Sudan-Egypt Border
articles.content_orig:
The Egyptian military and civilian police forces have launched the third phase of a joint security campaign targeting illegal gold prospecting across the Eastern Desert.
Authorities initiated this latest phase after dropping warning leaflets across targeted areas.
As noted by Egypt Today, the crackdown forms part of broader national efforts to "assert full sovereignty over Egyptian territory and protect the country's assets and natural resources" .
The ongoing military action comes amid recent media reports regarding alleged airstrikes near the southern border that reportedly resulted in casualties among informal artisanal miners.
In response to the reports, Sudan's Transitional Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan requested an official investigation to determine the origin and cause of the incident.
Addressing the situation, the Egyptian Armed Forces emphasized the enduring bond between both countries, stating that the peaceful presence of millions of Sudanese citizens in Egypt serves as "clear evidence of the longstanding relationship between the two nations ".
Egyptian Military leaders also advised residents across the region to rely on official news channels and "avoid being influenced by misleading rumors or foreign agendas seeking to undermine the fraternal ties between the Egyptian and Sudanese peoples" .
To reinforce bilateral stability, Egyptian Minister of Foreign Affairs Badr Abdelatty held a telephone conversation with Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieddin Salem.
Egypt today reported that Foreign Ministry spokesperson Nader Zaki confirmed that both officials underscored " the importance of mutual respect for each country's sovereignty, territorial integrity, and borders ".
Both governments reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining continuous consultations and cooperation, building upon recent bilateral talks between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi and General Abdel Fattah Al-Burhan.

articles.title_orig: Billboard names Music Industry Studies Program among world’s best
articles.title_zh: Billboard names Music Industry Studies Program among world’s best
articles.content_orig:
Over two back-to-back September weekends in Louisville, Kentucky, about a dozen University
                           of South Carolina students witnessed the behind-the-scenes challenges and drama inherent
                           in typical crowd-surfing outdoor rock music festivals. Make no mistake, though. Their
                           presence there was strictly business.
The entourage of students, accompanied by Jeremy Polley, assistant professor of music
                           industry studies, hit the ground running — running lights and sound, parsing logistics
                           and production issues, managing volunteers and troubleshooting all manner of scenarios
                           that can erupt in such environs. For credit.
That intensive, hands-on experiential learning through the multifaceted music industry
                           studies program at USC tops a long list of reasons Billboard magazine on Oct. 6 named it one of the very best in the country.
“Just seeing how many people it takes to put on these gigantic festivals was amazing.
                           There were easily about 1,000 employees,” senior Brianna Hale says of her time at
                           the recent Louder Than Life and Bourbon & Beyond festivals. “I was part of the guest
                           services team. We oversaw volunteers for the festival and accessibility, making sure
                           there were spaces for everyone.”
Polley says the number of music industry jobs is nearly infinite. Many people think
                           of music majors primarily as performers, but the coordination of talent it takes to
                           elevate those onstage and sustain their success is enormous.
“The students spent two weeks working side-by-side, networking, getting real-world
                           experience at the festivals,” he says. “That’s thanks to a partnership we’ve had for
                           five years with live music festival producer Danny Wimmer Presents (DWP). They have
                           hired some of our students right out of the program.”
The Billboard recognition comes while the young program is growing exponentially. Launched in 2021,
                           the music industry studies program includes tracks in record label management, recording
                           arts and live event production.
“To have national recognition shows that what we are doing here at USC is good work,
                           and it’s paying dividends,” Polley says. “We are training musicians to understand
                           the business side of the industry. They are not just learning songwriting, composition
                           and performance, but they are taking business, management and financial courses. They
                           are taking some recording courses. They are involved in live events.”
This is not like any music business program in America. We have built it so that you
                                          get instruction in a lot of different areas of the music industry ecosystem.
Music Dean Tayloe Harding is pleased with the program’s performance and how quickly
                           it has adapted, enabling students to tailor their interests through different concentrations
                           based on what part of the industry they want to pursue.
“This is not like any music business program in America. We have built it so that
                           you get instruction in a lot of different areas of the music industry ecosystem, making
                           you sort of a generalist,” Harding says, adding that the program’s versatility opens
                           many pathways for music students. “We saw how incredibly talented and diverse the
                           students were. That’s why we decided to build the tracks and make it a little more
                           individualized.”
Student Parker Craig likes that the program has evolved in lockstep with student needs.
                           It stays fresh by augmenting requisite classroom time with offsite learning opportunities
                           in authentic industry settings.
“The program is made to be built by students. They take our feedback, mold around
                           it and continue to create new and innovative learning experiences for us as students,”
                           Craig says. “I truly believe it to be one of the best decisions I ever could’ve made
                           in my life, and I’m so proud it’s getting the recognition it deserves.”
Like Hale, Craig found working at the DWP events to be some of his most memorable
                           immersions in the program.

                           have multiple connections not only within DWP but at different live event companies

Tucker Mullinax says it was a no-brainer to apply for the program because of its wide

                           Anaheim, California, for the National Association of Music Merchants (NAMM) convention
                           while still only a freshman.
“Through this trip, I was able to not only learn from and network with industry professionals,
                           but I was also able to get to know and become great friends with a lot of other students
                           on that trip,” he says. “I still look back on that being one of the most important

Polley says ideal music industry studies majors naturally embrace collaboration, are

articles.title_orig: 61-year-old woman holds plank for 5 hours in quest for new world record
articles.title_zh: 61-year-old woman holds plank for 5 hours in quest for new world record
articles.content_orig:
DonnaJean Wilde held a plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games earlier this month in Utah. It could be a new world record for longest plank held by a woman. But why does she do it?
And now, a world record attempt that's pretty hard to believe. DonnaJean Wilde, 61 years old, held a plank for exactly five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games earlier this month in Utah.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED CROWD: Four, three, two, one.
CHANG: Now, for those of you who are unfamiliar, a plank is an abdominal exercise where you hold your body in a rigid, straight line all the way from your head to your heels, supported only by your forearms and toes. Wilde already held the record for longest plank held by a woman, at four hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds. And she says she almost didn't make it past that mark this time.
DONNAJEAN WILDE: When I got to four hours and 30 minutes, I really did hit a wall. But with 10 minutes left or 15 minutes left, the CEO of the games, Kyle Case - he was on the mic, and he had that whole crowd cheering me, and that's why I made it through.
CHANG: Wilde's five-hour plank is currently under review by the experts at Guinness World Records. She says her love of the plank began about 15 years ago, when she had just broken her arm.
WILDE: I couldn't plank for very long - like, a minute, a minute and a half - but it was something I could do with a cast on, a broken wrist.
CHANG: But when the cast came off, she kept planking, and she kept getting better at it.
WILDE: And then my family - my kids, my husband - they said, you know, Mom, people don't do this. They don't get on the floor and just plank. So maybe you should, like, think about going for a record or something.
CHANG: Now, I know what you guys are all thinking out there. Why would someone choose to plank for so long? Well, for starters, Wilde says this kind of prolonged exercise gives her the same kind of rush as a runner's high. But also, she says, it's a good opportunity for multitasking.
WILDE: I completed a whole master's degree while I was planking, wrote all my papers. And I actually wrote a book.
CHANG: She is not kidding. She has apparently mastered the skill of typing on her laptop while propped up on her elbows, planking.
WILDE: As a teacher, so much of my life has been just trying to encourage people to find something that they love and then repeat it, because that just changes your brain.
CHANG: DonnaJean Wilde is pretty good at pushups, too, by the way. She once did 1,575 pushups in an hour, which was also a world record for a while. She says she might try and break that record again if she can find herself to take a break from all that planking.
(SOUNDBITE OF HVNSENT SONG, "SAVED MY SOUL")

Growers of giant pumpkins and their colossal gourds will gather on Monday in Northern California for an annual weighing competition, vying for the top award and a chance to challenge a world record set just last week in England .
At least 30 growers have registered for the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, south of San Francisco , according to event spokesman Ronan Fowler.
Among those competing is four-time champion Travis Gienger, a horticulture teacher from Minnesota whose winning run ended last year when he couldn't enter because his pumpkin split while still growing.
Gienger, who navigated freezing temperatures this growing season, produced a pumpkin with a circumference large enough to make it a potential world-record contender, Fowler said.
Fowler mentioned last week that Gienger and his father intended to alternate behind the wheel during a 30-hour drive over the weekend to deliver the small-car-sized pumpkin to California.
Ian Paton of Lymington, on the southern coast of England, set the existing world record with a giant squash weighing 2,857 pounds (1,296 kilograms). That figure exceeds the combined weight of two-and-a-half concert grand pianos.
Paton raises his massive gourds in a greenhouse, while Gienger cultivates his entries in a backyard pumpkin patch in Anoka, a city along the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis , Fowler noted.
"The fact that Travis can weather the elements, like 30-degree weather, and still grow this massive pumpkin is pretty unbelievable," the spokesman said.
Brandon Dawson, a resident of Santa Rosa , California, who won first place last year with a massive pumpkin weighing 2,346 pounds (1,064 kilograms), will also compete in the contest.
The winning grower this year will earn $9 for each pound of pumpkin and will have their giant gourd displayed during a parade through Half Moon Bay over the weekend. Should the winning entry surpass the world record, the competitor will receive an additional $30,000 prize.
Monday's proceedings, which mark the beginning of the city's autumn celebrations, will also feature a special appearance by pumpkin carver Mike Valladao.
However, these giant gourds are grown for size rather than flavor, so no oversized pumpkin pies will be served at the end of the event.

articles.title_orig: NASA’s Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven - NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) (.gov)
articles.title_zh: NASA’s Perseverance Sets Off-World Record for Total Distance Driven - NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) (.gov)
articles.content_orig:
This animated orbital-map view shows the route NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has taken from time of its 2021 landing to Oct. 11, 2026 — the day it broke the off-world driving record previously held by the agency’s Opportunity rover. As of that date, Perseverance has driven over 28 miles (45 kilometers).
The six-wheeled geologist has in less than six years surpassed a mark set by the agency’s Opportunity rover, which explored the Red Planet for nearly 15 years.
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover has driven farther than any vehicle ever has on the surface of another world. On Oct. 11, the rover’s odometer reached 28.10 miles (45.22 kilometers), eclipsing the record of 28.06 miles (45.16 kilometers) set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which explored Mars from 2004 to 2018. Perseverance reached the mark on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission, covering in five and a half years a distance that took Opportunity almost 15.
The milestone came as Perseverance traveled toward an area called “Idubi” through the region off the western rim of Jezero Crater nicknamed “Lac de Charmes,” where the rover is investigating what may be some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system. The rocks and terrain of Lac de Charmes are so ancient that their Earthly equivalents have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics (Mars doesn’t have tectonic plates), and Idubi is where the science team hopes to find traces of ancient hydrothermal systems.
Much of the credit belongs to Perseverance’s self-driving capability. Using an autonomous navigation system known as AutoNav , the rover images the terrain while rolling, builds a 3D map of hazards, and plots its course between waypoints selected by rover planners on Earth — a capability the team calls “thinking while driving.” Perseverance can do all that at or near its top speed , covering as much as 1,351 feet (412 meters) in a single sol. The six-wheeled scientist has driven more than 90% of its total distance using AutoNav to evaluate the terrain, compared with about 5% for the first Martian AutoNav system on Opportunity and its twin, Spirit. Where NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner , assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points, Perseverance processes 600,000 with every look.
One of Perseverance’s navigation cameras captured this shot on Oct. 11, 2026, the Martian day, or sol, that a 299.6-foot (91.31-meter) drive pushed the rover’s total mileage past Opportunity’s 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) record on Mars.
“It is an honor to be working on Perseverance at a moment when the technology has evolved to the point that drives like these are routine,” said Steven Lee, the project manager of the Curiosity and Perseverance rovers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “The original mission called for no more than 12.4 miles of driving. We’ve blown well past that, and with all mobility systems fully operational and favorable extended-ground-life test results, we expect Perseverance to keep adding to this record for many years to come.”
NASA recently approved the mission’s first extension, which began in October and will carry Perseverance’s exploration of the crater rim through roughly the end of 2028.
Perseverance’s record caps nearly three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars, each mission driving farther and more capably than the last.
The microwave-oven-size Sojourner rover covered about 330 feet (100 meters) during its 83-sol mission in 1997. The golf-cart-size twins Spirit and Opportunity arrived in 2004 with 90-sol prime missions. Spirit logged 4.8 miles (7.7 kilometers) before succumbing to the Martian winter in 2010. Opportunity kept rolling for 5,111 sols, completing the first extraterrestrial marathon in 2015 and setting the record Perseverance has now surpassed. The agency’s Curiosity rover, which landed in Gale Crater in 2012 and remains hard at work, has logged more than 23.65 miles (38.07 kilometers).
“The rover that broke this record did so by making its own decisions about the path. Given the autonomy to just go, Perseverance is a better driver than the one that landed, and we’re not done,” Mark Maimone, deputy team chief for robotic operations on Perseverance. “Our newest software teaches Perseverance to steer less and roll more, and to check its own position against orbital maps mid-drive. The next frontier is sunlight itself. Glare in the navigation cameras is why we park by mid-afternoon if we’re driving toward the Sun, and if we can teach the rover to see past those artifacts, every rover that follows gets a longer working day.”
This infographic illustrates the distances driven by various rovers on the surface of Earth’s Moon and Mars. Of the vehicles shown, the NASA Mars rovers Perseverance and Curiosity are still operational and moving across the surface; the figures shown for those two are distances driven as of Oct. 11, 2026.
The extraterrestrial off-road driving record isn’t limited to Mars: Lunar driving records were broken earlier in the journey. Perseverance rolled past both the 22.2 miles (35.7 kilometers) covered by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in 1972 and the 24.2 miles (39 kilometers) driven by the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973.
Setting distance records is just a bonus. Stamina and longer drives are putting more geologic diversity within reach faster — more outcrops examined and more of the Red Planet’s history read from its rocks. That reach carried Perseverance from an ancient lakebed up a fossilized river system, where the rover found a potential biosignature at a rock called “Cheyava Falls,” and on to the crater rim, where an entirely different kind of ancient habitat — hydrothermal — may await.
Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples spanning the crater floor, a delta fan formed by a long-gone river, and now the crater rim. In the latter region, it has been exploring impact-generated rocks some 4 billion years old, from a chapter of planetary history almost entirely erased on Earth.
After Lac de Charmes, the rover will continue along the crater rim and head south during the extended mission towards Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide (100-meter-wide) block of ancient crust uplifted by the impact that created Jezero.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.
Managed for NASA by Caltech, JPL built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. JPL also built PIXL and SHERLOC.

articles.title_orig: The University of California is a world leader, according to this new global ranking
articles.title_zh: The University of California is a world leader, according to this new global ranking
articles.content_orig:
At home and abroad, the UC system is unrivaled. That’s according to new rankings from Times Higher Education, a U.K.-based publication.
The World University 2027 rankings identified UC’s nine undergraduate campuses as among the best 50 public universities in the United States. Six UC campuses are among the nation’s top 40, private or public, and all nine undergraduate campuses are among the top 20% of all universities around the world.
The rankings evaluate five main factors — teaching, research, the economic footprint of that research, and international staff, students and research collaborations — across a pool of 2,297 universities in 118 countries and territories.
*The World University rankings group universities into bands after the top 200.
The University of California is at the very top of a variety of rankings. Those include rankings of student outcomes ( Forbes ), global reputation ( U.S. News ), universities that produce startups ( Pitchbook ) and the U.S. News Best Colleges rankings , which have named a University of California campus the nation’s top public every year since its 1999 edition.
The Times Higher Education World University ranking originated in 2004. It’s named UC Berkeley the top public university in the U.S. for 11 of the past 12 years.

UC’s real-world impact is exemplified by the winners of the inaugural UC Regents Innovation Awards.

articles.title_orig: Russia Lab Death Sparks Plague Fears in China
articles.title_zh: Russia Lab Death Sparks Plague Fears in China
articles.content_orig:
Social media speculation that a suspected plague outbreak in Russia could spread to China has reportedly prompted some residents there to stock up on food and supplies.
The U.K.'s Daily Star reported people were scrambling for rice, sugar, eggs, canned food, and other necessities over fears of COVID-style lockdowns.
The report pointed to social media claims rather than any confirmed cases in China.
The Oct. 2 death of a 28-year-old worker at a Russian institute in Irkutsk that studies plagues led to a quarantine response involving at least 200 people.
Russia has denied she died of plague, saying she died of pneumonia.
Dr. Amesh Adalja, a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, said Sunday on Newsmax the case could involve something more dangerous than plague.
"What worried me was the response of the Russians, the 200 people that were being monitored, the quarantining of a hospital, the hazmat suits," Adalja said on " Wake Up America Weekend ." "That type of reaction made me think this was something worse than plague."
He noted that plague today is "a pretty treatable infection" that does not spread rapidly from person to person.
Adalja also cited the Soviet Union's secret biological weapons program, which he said included its plague research institutes and which "we think has resumed."
The World Health Organization said in a report Saturday that Russia reported negative tests for plague and other high-threat diseases and no additional linked cases, but the cause of death remains undetermined.
Adalja said Russia's denial could be accurate.
"But we still don't know what killed her, what they were testing for, what they were suspicious of," he said. "And I don't know if we'll ever get good answers."
