articles.title_orig: Congress Says Webull Is Structurally Tied to China, Stock Craters
articles.title_zh: Congress Says Webull Is Structurally Tied to China, Stock Craters
articles.content_orig:
Hunan Weibu, Webull's mainland China subsidiary, employs 863 people, 62% of its global workforce, according to the House committee, directly contradicting the company's earlier claim of having no PRC-based staff.
A House panel just told millions of Webull users their trading app answers to more than Wall Street. The stock lost nearly a fifth of its value in a single session.
Webull shares opened at $5.15 on October 7. By midday the stock was down as much as 32%. CNBC had reported that the bipartisan House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party had concluded the trading platform is "tied in structural ways" to Beijing. By the close, the stock had pared some of the damage but still finished down roughly 19.1% at $5.89. For a brokerage that leans on retail traders checking balances between work meetings, that's not a bad headline. That's a run on trust.
The committee's report, chaired by Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan alongside ranking member Raja Krishnamoorthi, didn't accuse Webull of being a shell company. It did something more specific and, for a US-listed app with millions of accounts, more damaging: it laid out a "profound gap" between how Webull presents itself and who actually runs the machine behind it. Moolenaar put it bluntly on CNBC, saying China-based operations "put American investors and their data at risk" because they expose that data to Chinese government authorities.
The specifics are where the report does its real work. According to the committee, Webull's mainland Chinese subsidiary, Hunan Weibu, employs 863 people, which the panel says amounts to 62% of the company's entire global workforce. That number matters because Webull had previously told committee members it "does not have any offices or employees based in the People's Republic of China," a claim the new headcount figure directly contradicts. The committee also flagged software development, data pipelines and core engineering operations. Cross-border data routing, financing and compliance made the list too: all of it dependent on infrastructure governed by Chinese law, meaning Beijing can compel cooperation from the entities that keep the app running.
This isn't a cold case the committee just stumbled into. Moolenaar and Krishnamoorthi first wrote to Webull CEO Anthony Denier back in December 2024. They warned that the company's ties to PRC-based entities raised questions about US user data security and Webull's ability to comply with American regulations. Webull was founded in 2016 under Hunan Fumi Information Technology, a China-based fintech venture started by Wang Anquan, before the company restructured and pushed its public identity toward Florida and New York. The gap between that founding and today's marketing is exactly what the committee spent nearly two years examining.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tesla is weighing a sale or spinoff of its China business to enable a SpaceX merger. Elon Musk called it absurdly fake news. Tesla stock jumped 2.7% overnight and gave most of it back after the denial, leaving investors to decide who to believe. - tesla china spinoff rumors explained - elon musk tesla stock denial impact
Webull disputes the findings. A company spokesperson said Webull "made every effort to cooperate with the Committee, but did not hear from them for more than 20 months before this report was released." The spokesperson called the conclusions "deeply disappointing," citing "significant inaccuracies and unsupported conclusions." The company maintains its US operations run out of its Florida and New York offices, that US customer data sits on US infrastructure, and that access to sensitive systems is controlled domestically.
Here's the problem with that defense: the committee isn't arguing Webull lied about where its American offices sit. It's arguing that the engineering and data plumbing behind the app, the part users never see, runs through a subsidiary Beijing can lean on by law. A US address doesn't settle that question. Neither side disputes that Hunan Weibu exists or that it's large; the dispute is over what that size means for who actually controls the product.
Webull went public through a SPAC merger in April 2025. Since then it's spent the time trying to look like any other US retail brokerage, chasing the same customers as Robinhood and SoFi with zero-commission trades and extended-hours access. A congressional report questioning its structural independence from a foreign adversary government is the kind of headline that outlasts a single trading session. Regulators scrutinizing TikTok set the template here: ownership structure and data routing, not marketing copy, are what Washington is going to keep testing.
For StartupFortune readers weighing retail brokerages or any US-listed fintech with cross-border roots, the Webull episode is a reminder. A Nasdaq listing and a Florida mailing address don't settle questions about who controls the backend. Where the code runs and who can compel the people running it increasingly matters as much as where the logo sits.

articles.title_orig: Massive Anoka pumpkin to be carved into world?s largest jack-o-lantern
articles.title_zh: Massive Anoka pumpkin to be carved into world?s largest jack-o-lantern
articles.content_orig:
Travis Gienger of Anoka, Minnesota, showing off his five championship rings from the World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off. (Safeway World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off / Supplied)
HALF MOON BAY, Calif. (FOX 9) - Minnesota's Travis Gienger won the World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in California for the fifth time, with his pumpkin, "Rocky", taking home the grand prize.
Rocky weighed in at 2,389 pounds on Monday at the 2026 World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, California, the heaviest pumpkin in the competition. Rocky also measured 138 inches side-to-side, 131.5 inches end-to-end and 231 inches around.
But Gienger's giant pumpkin didn't break the world record. The current world record for heaviest pumpkin is 2,856 pounds, set on Oct. 3 by a British pumpkin grower. A pumpkin grower in Rhode Island may have surpassed that record on Saturday with his pumpkin that weighed in at 3,156 pounds, although it does not appear that record has been certified yet.
Gienger earned $900 per pound for his pumpkin—which adds up to $2,151.
The city of Anoka is saying go big or gourd home. A champion pumpkin grown in Anoka is expected to break two Guinness World Records this week. Anoka, affectionately known as the Halloween Capital of the World, prides itself on its Halloween celebrations and now has yet another Halloween accolade to celebrate. North America's largest pumpkin is on display at Anoka City Hall, where it will be carved into the world's largest jack-o-lantern by weight and by size on Friday.
This was the 53rd World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off. Gienger has now won the grand prize five times. Here's how his other prize-winning pumpkins compare:
In 2022, Gienger's championship pumpkin, Maverick, was carved into the world's largest jack-o-lantern . The pumpkin was displayed outside Anoka City Hall.
The World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off began in 1974 as a friendly challenge between Half Moon Bay and Circleville, Ohio to see who could grow the biggest pumpkin.
The Source: The 2026 Safeway World Championship Pumpkin Weigh-Off in Half Moon Bay, California took place on Monday, Oct. 12. The event was livestreamed on YouTube. FOX 9 reported this story from Minnesota.

articles.title_orig: Starbucks says not buying Chipotle, ends takeover speculation
articles.title_zh: Starbucks says not buying Chipotle, ends takeover speculation
articles.content_orig:
Starbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover.
"Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer.
Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.
The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies.
On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.
Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025 , when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.
The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports.
Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

articles.title_orig: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.title_zh: Why Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire
articles.content_orig:
On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly.
Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed.
Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up – if Russia does.
Russia is saying: Very little.
Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists.
"Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied.
"As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you."
Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has.
It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow.
"Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded.
"It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery.
"That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway.
"But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have.
"In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it."
In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's.
In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country.
Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests – as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November.
Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel .
Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices.
Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv.
Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv.
It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine.
"The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said.
"Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that.
On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections.
That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer.
It comes as no surprise though.
Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting.
Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine.
On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting.
On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning.
"This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written.
The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation.
Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal.

articles.title_orig: PODCAST: Omar raid, diesel deal pushback, prediction markets (Updated)
articles.title_zh: PODCAST: Omar raid, diesel deal pushback, prediction markets (Updated)
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism .
Trump, in a Truth Social post , accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union.
"The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote.
While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy.
"I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.
Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months.
The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin , ends the war against Ukraine.
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.
Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal.
"While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.
Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent , however.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

articles.title_orig: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.title_zh: Victims of Pennsylvania mass shooting included pregnant daughter of gunman
articles.content_orig:
The victims of a mass shooting in northwest Pennsylvania included the gunman’s wife and pregnant daughter, who was due to give birth Monday, authorities said.
Matthew Stone , 45, died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound Friday after he opened fire at his home on Perry Street in Erie, Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook told NBC News on Monday.
Victims included Stone’s wife, Michelle Stone, 44; daughter, Angelina K. Stone, 24, who was pregnant; and sons Matthew Stone Jr., 21, and Jonathan Stone, 19, Cook said.
Angelina Stone was carrying “an unborn fetus who was supposed to have been born today,” Cook said.
Two other unidentified children, a 5-year-old boy and a nearly 2-year-old girl, who were also related to the shooter were killed inside the house, according to the coroner.
All six of those victims were found in the house, where they lived, while victims Twila A. Tanner, 51, and Lora Lee Roberts, 37, were fatally shot outside, Cook said.
Roberts was Michelle Stone’s sister and had gone to the house Friday at the request of Angelina Stone, who needed a ride to the hospital, said the victim’s friend Christine Tombaugh.
Tanner was a friend and neighbor of Roberts, and they lived just a few miles from the crime scene, Tombaugh said.
Roberts was active in local homeless advocacy work, so answering a relative’s call for help and bringing along a friend for assistance was typical of her kindness, Tombaugh said.
“Absolutely, that’s who she was,” said Tombaugh, executive director of the homeless shelter Community of Caring .
“Her passion in life was helping others. She had a giving spirit, a beautiful heart,” Tombaugh said. “Great mom, just a valued friend. She had a heart for the homeless and people in need, just helping whoever she could. That was her passion.”
Juicesiyah Alexander Ezekiel , the slain girl’s father, said he is struggling to understand why the elder Stone opened fire.
“I wouldn’t even put this on my worst enemy, man,” Ezekiel told NBC affiliate WICU of Erie. “It’s sickening.”
The girl was going to turn 2 next month.
“Her name is Amari’anna,” Ezekiel said. “She’s the most beautiful baby God could have created.”

articles.title_orig: ‘VisionQuest’ Rotten Tomatoes Reviews Are Mostly In Tune With New Marvel Series
articles.title_zh: ‘VisionQuest’ Rotten Tomatoes Reviews Are Mostly In Tune With New Marvel Series
articles.content_orig:
Partway through “ VisionQuest ,” the titular android Vision (Paul Bettany) attempts to help a British teenager named Tommy (Ruaridh Mollica) understand the precise nature of their relationship. The truth goes something like this: Vision is a reconstituted version of his former self, who was killed by Thanos in “Avengers: Infinity War” and then kinda-sorta brought back sans memories by his wife Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen), a grieving witch, in the 2021 series “WandaVision”; Tommy is an ordinary person suddenly imbued with the consciousness and abilities of a child Wanda invented with magic, which survived the collapse of his mother’s suburban simulation and crossed the pond in search of a host.
Vision runs a simulation where he struggles, over and over again, to condense all this lore and explain it to Tommy in a way that doesn’t overwhelm him with anger and confusion. There’s not a single version that doesn’t end with Tommy storming out of the room.
This is more or less how it feels to watch “VisionQuest,” an eight-episode Marvel Studios series that’s positioned as a sequel of sorts to “WandaVision.” The show plays with some clever concepts, particularly in its visual presentation; as the simulation scenarios pile up, so do Vision clones until a dozen exhausted, exasperated Bettanys all collapse on a hotel floor. (Much of “VisionQuest” strips away the monochrome coating to show Vision as an ordinary human, allowing Bettany to flex his fusty charm.) But this imagery is larded with so much convoluted backstory and abstract concepts that “VisionQuest” ends up in the exact same predicament as Vision himself, a synthetic being trying and mostly failing to connect with his emotions.
Artificial intelligence has long been a staple of comics and other forms of science fiction, but as real-life AI companies talk seriously about potential sentience, there’s a topical slant to Vision’s preferred strategy for getting in touch with his feelings. He’s created and/or convened a bunch of autonomous AIs — what we would now call “agents,” though creator Terry Matalas may have overseen the scripts before that term fully entered the popular lexicon — to help him with various tasks. There’s F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), who helps decode social interactions, and E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), who’s a proponent of fun. Mechanics D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis) and U (Jonathan Sayer) tend to the more mundane work of keeping internal systems in shape. Finally, there are more familiar figures from earlier stages of the MCU: Tony Stark’s old pal J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy) is on hand; most intriguingly, so is Ultron (James Spader), the namesake antagonist of the second “Avengers” film.
All these assistants take corporeal form in Vision’s so-called Mindspace, a virtual and psychological plane that takes the shape of a quirky Victorian mansion. Here, Ultron looks not like a menacing CGI robot but the 66-year-old Spader himself: a schlubby guy with a flowing beard and a trenchcoat whose menacing, purple-prosed monologues (“It feels to me like your Greek tragedy has a deuteragonist”) are undercut by his appearance. To the show’s credit, this Ultron is a highly entertaining creation, allowing Spader to layer some of his signature sardonic air to a character who’s still cynical, but much humbled from his supervillain days. Without access to the real world, Ultron has to settle for being the devil on Vision’s shoulder rather than an actor in his own right.
It’s when the Mindspace intersects with said real world that “VisionQuest” gets overly complicated. Directors Christopher J. Byrne, Gandja Monteiro and Vincenzo Natali — along with Matalas, who helms the final pair of episodes — have some fun inside that mutable dimension: When a hostile android’s neural network connects with Vision’s, the episode becomes a riff on possession and exorcism (“The power of code compels you!”), and when Ultron begs Vision to let him “take the wheel,” it’s a literal ship’s wheel buffeted by stormwinds. But apart from having the AIs appear and speak to Vision as a kind of imaginary friend, invisible to everyone else, “VisionQuest” never lands on a consistent or legible way to map the relationship between the two realms, or how events in one affect the material reality of the other.
Constantly toggling between the Mindspace and meatspace (sorry, it’s right there!) inevitably takes a toll on Tommy, who only exists in the latter. Even by the fantastical standards of comics-based storytelling, the tenuousness of Tommy’s nature — he’s kind of another incarnation of Quicksilver, played by Evan Peters in “WandaVision,” but also kind of not? — makes him a difficult protagonist to map onto. That straining to comprehend the irrational fog of human emotions is the show’s explicit subject only clarifies the problem rather than neutralizing it. As Vision wonders what his purpose is without Wanda or the Avengers, we do, too.
“VisionQuest” tries to balance such philosophical questions about consciousness (yes, the Ship of Theseus metaphor comes back) with more active conflicts. At the behest of a mysterious client, the bounty hunter Paladin (Todd Stashwick) is on Vision’s trail, as is the aforementioned android (T’Nia Miller). Evading them provides some momentum, though not enough to propel an entire cast so massive I haven’t even mentioned Diane “Philomena Cunk” Morgan, who plays the Paladin’s assistant, yet. Before long, “VisionQuest” is trying to stitch all its unwieldy threads together with basic clichés about chosen family. “VisionQuest” often tells the audience what we’re supposed to be feeling, yet rarely achieves its stated aim.
“WandaVision” was the first Marvel Studios show to air on Disney+, and with its shapeshifting sitcom homage as an allegory for grief, that series has remained a high bar to beat amid the MCU’s oversaturation era. This remains the case for the direct sequel. “VisionQuest” rehashes many of the same themes about recovering from loss — there is, of course, a flashback to the famous line about love persevering — with a hero who is, by definition, much less accessible. (And given AI’s alarming trajectory toward mass job replacement and/or civilizational destruction, I didn’t feel especially inclined to empathize with a bunch of digital entities.) “VisionQuest” can be enjoyable in its comfort zone of zanily tweaking the Mindspace. But when it’s time to venture out into the tactile world, the show doesn’t leave a lasting mark.
The first two episodes of “VisionQuest” will premiere on Disney+ on Oct. 14, with remaining episodes airing weekly on Wednesdays.

Luxury retail company LVMH saw quarterly sales slump following a trademark dispute in China.
Organic revenue for the company’s fashion and leather goods unit fell 5% year over year in the third quarter, LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton announced in a Monday (Oct. 12) press release, with the company’s total revenue for the quarter up 1%.
Louis Vuitton sales suffered in China after the company achieved a victory in a trademark battle with local tea company Molly Tea , Bloomberg reported Monday. This led to backlash from Chinese consumers, angry that the world’s biggest luxury company would take a much smaller merchant to court.

Sales in the region including China dipped 5% in the quarter, the report said, marking the only area where LVMH saw negative performance, the report said. The company’s American depositary receipts dropped as much as 3.6% in New York following the release of the numbers.
LVMH’s stock is down more than 40% this year, on pace for the company’s worst yearly performance since 2008’s global financial crisis, according to the report. Gucci’s revenue fell 5% on a comparable basis in the first half of 2026, including a 6% drop at directly operated stores, PYMNTS reported Sept. 17. Second-quarter comparable revenue was still down 2% despite an uptick from the first quarter. Department stores were working to get customers “to spend more without making the jump into luxury,” according to the report, which cited increased sales at Macy’s and Dillard’s .
“For department stores, the difference between moving upmarket and moving into luxury is consequential to the size of the customer base they can address,” the report said.
Meanwhile, the PYMNTS Intelligence report “ The Smart Basket Opportunity: Why Issuers Are Ready For A Better Rewards System ” found in June that 56% of issuers and FinTechs said their card rewards increased average spend per transaction, 61% said they boosted total spending and 66% reported an increase in card use frequency.

articles.title_orig: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Energy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Oil and gas prices rose Monday after an “energy ceasefire” announced by President Donald Trump on Sunday failed to gain traction.
Brent crude oil jumped 2% to almost $108 per barrel and U.S. crude oil rose more than 2% to about $94. Meanwhile, diesel futures fully erased a small drop they saw last week.
Just weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the price pressures are mounting. Republicans face a steep climb to maintain their majorities in Congress, and voters across the country cite high gas prices as a key issue affecting their votes.
The average nationwide price of diesel fuel Monday was $6.26 per gallon, nearly 80% higher than it had been at the start of the year, according to AAA data.
The rising prices Monday came less than 24 hours after Trump declared that a ceasefire had been agreed to.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social .
Shortly after the president’s post, Russia renewed strikes against Ukrainian energy assets.
Pressed by reporters Monday as to why neither the Kremlin nor Kyiv had firmly committed to his ceasefire, Trump indicated that he knew when he made the announcement on Sunday that he did not yet have a commitment from either side.
“They agreed, you know why? Because I said ‘You agree,” Trump told reporters at the White House. As for getting Russian President Vladimir Putin to commit, Trump said, “We’re going to see what happens.”
Asked if he was aware that Russia had already violated the ceasefire Trump had announced, the president replied, “I’m not sure about that,” before claiming there had been “violations on both sides.”
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine learned about Trump’s ceasefire from media reports and was given no advance warning. He reiterated his position that Ukraine was open to an agreement not to target enemy energy infrastructure as long as Moscow agrees to it, too.
In the meantime, Russia continued with “glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said Monday, noting that a power plant in Kharkiv had recently been attacked.
“Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them — ‘nyet,’” Zelenskyy said, using the Russian word for “no.”
The Kremlin on Monday neither confirmed nor denied having agreed to a deal.
Trump’s Sunday announcement closely mirrored a similar post he made in September, when he announced that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
There, too, Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s participation hinged on Russia’s agreement to comply, which never came. Neither Ukrainian nor Russian strikes on the other’s energy assets slowed down in September.
The dubious ceasefire Trump declared over the weekend followed a stunning announcement Friday in which the president said Russia would supply millions of barrels of diesel “to the American and Global Marketplace.”
The announcement came after a phone call Friday between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin that reportedly lasted over an hour.
Trump said the deal with Putin would “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” That would translate into about 2.25 million barrels of diesel, or less diesel than the United States uses in just one day.
Further details and logistics of Russia’s plan had yet to be announced Monday.
In addition to the Russia deal, Trump has pressured G7 allies to release more diesel fuel supplies in recent days and lifted domestic restrictions on an off-road variety of diesel.
In order to clear a legal path for the diesel deal, the Treasury Department announced a six-month suspension of the fuel sanctions imposed on the Kremlin in 2022 for its illegal invasion of Ukraine.
Ukrainian officials, European allies and some U.S. lawmakers were aghast at the deal and the U.S. decision to unilaterally ease Russia sanctions.
Trump defended the deal Monday , calling it “the right choice for the American People.”
Trump also said more diesel fuel would be made available “within a short period of time,” if Russia’s refineries could produce it.
Yet experts are highly skeptical that there will be any significant resumption of Russian diesel exports in the near term.
Due to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia , refiners that produce oil, gas and diesel have suffered heavy damage.
“Reported gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%, prompting the government to restrict fuel exports to protect domestic supplies,” analysts at the International Energy Agency wrote in a September report.
For weeks, Trump has focused on the price of diesel fuel, which began rising as a result of the Iran war that the U.S. and Israel launched in February.
In July, escalations in the Russia-Ukraine war began adding to the pressure on diesel prices.
As Ukrainian drones systematically targeted Russian energy assets, the Kremlin responded by restricting diesel exports in order to preserve its supply for domestic use.
Until then, Russia had been one of the world’s top exporters of refined oil products, which include diesel fuel.
Russia said Friday that it would lift some of its export restrictions in order to accommodate the deal with Trump. But it was unclear how fast that would happen.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: West Coast mom of six loses both legs, hand after doctors ignored her complaints: bombshell lawsuit
articles.title_zh: West Coast mom of six loses both legs, hand after doctors ignored her complaints: bombshell lawsuit
articles.content_orig:
After a undergoing a routine hysterectomy, Trisha Stevens was eager to return to normal.
But just weeks later, the Oregon mother of six would battle a debilitating infection — leading her to lose both both of her legs, one of her hands, and face other life-changing complications.
Now, Trisha and her husband Brian are suing multiple Portland-area doctors and regional healthcare giant Legacy Health, seeking $68.5 million in damages, KGW reports.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
“I came home having lost both of my legs and my right hand,” Trisha told KGW. “My left hand was left unusable after the necrosis. I lost parts of my lips and tongue, and I live with paralysis in a body that no longer responds the way it once did.”
Trisha’s nightmare reportedly began with a hysterectomy — performed by Dr. Alvin Nakamura on October 4. 2024 at Adventist Health in Portland. Four days after her surgery, pathology results showed inflammation. But there is no record Dr. Nakamura ever reviewed the results, informed Trisha, or took any steps to address the inflammation, according to the lawsuit.
Around two weeks after the surgery, Trisha experience a sharp pain in her abdomen followed by vaginal bleeding while walking down the bleachers at her son’s softball game
She called Dr. Nakamura’s clinic, Bridgetown Medical Group, and reported continued bleeding, a blood clot “the size of a baseball,” a low-grade fever, diarrhea and stomach cramping.
Through a nurse, Nakamura told Trisha to monitor her bleeding at home and come into the office if she passed another clot, but her condition quickly worsened.
Later that night, when Trisha arrived to the emergency room at Legacy Mount Hood, her heart was racing, her blood pressure, low and she was breathing quickly. According to the lawsuit, she was “saturating vaginal pads with blood at a rate of three per hour.”
Hospital staff diagnosed Trisha with peritonitis, an inflammation of the abdominal lining; lactic acidosis, a buildup of acid in the blood; and acute kidney injury. Later, she was diagnosed with bacteria in the bloodstream and septic shock.
The hospital’s on-call OB/GYN Dr. Gregory Eilers then noted that the edges of Trisha’s surgical closure were separated and looked raw, diagnosing her with an infection at the site. Despite this, the doctor did not recommend surgery or test for infection inside the abdomen, according to the lawsuit.
The suit also claims that once Trisha was admitted to the hospital, the infection continued to spread, leading to multiple organ failure.
Over the next several weeks, both of Trisha’s legs were amputated above the knee, and her right hand was amputated at the wrist. Her left thumb and portions of her left finger also needed to be removed.
Due to tissue necrosis, Trisha also lost portions of her lips and tongue, much of her hair, and suffered spinal cord damage, leaving her paraplegic.
“There are days I still do not know which was harder: almost dying or waking up and realizing everything that was taken from me,” Trisha told KGW.
“I was a wife who could reach for Brian’s hand without thinking and a mother who could walk down the hallway when one of my children called my name,”  she continued.
“I could climb into bed beside them after a nightmare, wrap both arms around them when they cried, and make them feel safe simply by being there. I could drive, cook, clean, care for my family and carry my share of our life. I never knew those ordinary things were freedoms until they were gone.”
Now, Trisha’s husband Brian acts as her caretaker.
The complications have led to a profound change in Trisha’s daily life. The mom told KGW she can no longer play with her children or navigate her home with ease, as it is not built to accommodate a wheelchair.
“Even the gravel driveway I crossed thousands of times without a second thought can stop my wheelchair from following my family outside,” Trisha said.
“I fought so hard to survive because I wanted to come home to them. I never imagined that I could make it home and still sometimes feel as though I am living on the edge of the very life I fought so hard to return to.”
In the lawsuit, Trisha claims Legacy Health staff were negligent in delaying treatment of the abdominal infection and in managing her blood pressure.
It also claims Nakamura and Bridgetown Medical were negligent in not evaluating her or sending her to emergency care after she reported her symptoms following her hysterectomy.
The mom told KGW that of the most difficult parts of her complications is losing her independance.
“I did not fight this hard simply to remain alive while life happens around me,” Stevens said. “I survived because I desperately want to live it and God saved me!”

articles.title_orig: Trump's top NATO general: 'We will fight' if Russia attacks Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump's top NATO general: 'We will fight' if Russia attacks Europe
articles.content_orig:
He said it’s 'up to our people' in response to Trump’s call for new elections.
After President Donald Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil refineries, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy defended the attacks in an exclusive interview with ABC News, saying his country is responding to repeated Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"I said it to President Trump … to his team and to his people several times: we want peace, we are ready for [a] ceasefire, we are ready to begin from any kind of steps of de-escalation," Zelenskyy told "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl. "And if the Russians want us not [to] attack their diesel, their refineries and etc., we are asking President Trump, give them signal not attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine."
He went on, "Don't attack us. Don't kill our children. We will stop attack[ing] your diesel. And I think it's [a] fair, fair deal."
After Zelenskyy’s interview on ABC News aired, Trump said on social media that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to an energy ceasefire.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” his post said.
Zelenskyy and his office were not informed about Trump’s statement of an energy ceasefire with Russia ahead of time and learned about it from social media, a senior source in Ukraine's presidential office told ABC News.
The source said Ukraine has no information about the alleged agreement.
On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Zelenskyy to reporters, claiming the Ukrainian president "chooses not to" end the war with Russia, which began when Russia invaded the sovereign country in February of 2022.
Amid a global energy crisis, Trump took issue with Ukraine's repeated strikes on Russian oil refineries, asserting that those strikes are exacerbating the price of diesel.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused. And [Zelenskyy] wants to make problems for the world," Trump said. "He can do whatever he wants. But you can't do that because we have a world problem. And the problem is caused by the lack of refineries for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits refineries."
A senior Ukrainian source told ABC News that Ukraine expects the Trump administration to stop sharing U.S. intelligence that tracks Russian missile launches in retaliation over Kyiv’s refusal to end strikes on Russia’s oil industry.
Trump and Zelenskyy have had a tumultuous relationship. In 2025, a meeting in the Oval Office with reporters devolved into a shouting match before the cameras, with Trump and Vice President JD Vance rebuking the Ukrainian president for his handling of the war and even falsely blaming Zelenskyy for beginning the conflict.
The latest spat comes after Trump announced the U.S. had made a deal with Russia to "immediately" import 300,000 tons of its diesel fuel, with a promise that millions more are coming.
Zelenskyy said this deal amounts to an "obvious weakness."
"It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said. "We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one."
Less than 24 hours later, Trump called for Zelenskyy to be replaced.
"You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made many deals. And for some reason, he never does," Trump said on the White House South Lawn. "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
He later told reporters, "I think he should have an election."
Responding to those comments, Zelenskyy told Karl, "With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader."
Zelenskyy also offered a solution that he said was shared with the Trump administration: a commitment to hold elections if Russian President Vladimir Putin abides by a 60-day ceasefire.
“I know that Putin wanted very much to change the president in Ukraine, I understand it. And if President Trump really wants to have some changes in -- during elections, I also shared it with his team: please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days of total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections. Of course, we will be ready for any choice of our people.”
Karl asked Zelenskyy why he thinks Trump and Elon Musk, whose Starlink internet is essential for Ukraine, are blaming him for the war’s continuation. Musk said Saturday on X that Zelenskyy has “gone too far.”
“Because these people can't find a key how to stop Putin,” Zelenskyy said. “Because it's more simple to speak about the prices and connect it with Ukraine when everybody in the world understands ... prices are rising … because of the war in Middle East, of the blocking of Hormuz, because of these reasons. Everybody understands it.”
Asked how long Ukraine can continue to defend itself as the war approaches five years, Zelenskyy said the war has to end.
“I hope that we will save this unity, Europe and the United States," he said. "We will defend ourselves because otherwise, we will lose our life and homes, our freedom, independence, Ukraine. Yeah, we can't lose it. And the truth is on our side."

articles.title_orig: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.title_zh: The US needs its own grey-zone tactics in the South China Sea - The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.source: The Strategist | ASPI's analysis and commentary site
articles.content_orig:
Passive resistance to Beijing’s actions in the South China Sea is not working. If the United States wants to win in the region, it needs a grey-zone strategy of its own.
Beijing has spent a decade refining a playbook that stays deliberately below the threshold of armed conflict. Chinese coast guard ships ram Philippine vessels, maritime militia swarm disputed reefs, and drones shadow foreign ships. Washington’s response – patrols, joint statements and expressions of concern – has imposed few costs and changed little.
This passivity means that China isn’t being deterred. Indeed, it’s being reassured that it can keep getting away with what it’s doing.
The US doesn’t need ships built for ramming to change that calculation. Rather, it should play to its strengths: a vast intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance network, powerful cyber and electromagnetic warfare capabilities and a web of regional partners. The US military’s F3EAD targeting cycle (find, fix, finish, exploit, analyse and disseminate) offers a template for response. For grey-zone competition, it can be adapted into F2RED: find, fix, respond, exploit and disseminate, with calibrated non-kinetic responses replacing the kinetic component (the ‘finish’).
The first two steps of the cycle that could be applied to the South China Sea are largely in place. Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance assets across the region already track Chinese coast guard, navy, and maritime militia vessels, and coordination with partner forces can expand the network even further. But after that there’s a gap, because of Washington’s reticence to respond with any operation that may cause escalation.
One response below the threshold of armed conflict is to apply soft-kill effects – that is, nothing with kinetic impact, at least not on anything very costly or with people in it. When Chinese vessels launch uncrewed aircraft to harass or surveil ships of US partners, allied forces can jam or bring down the drones on the spot. Operations can be conducted against Chinese drones elsewhere to divert Beijing’s attention from the area of tension. The same tools become more potent against larger, more expensive ships and aircraft. Crucially, these effects must be paired with signalling, making it clear to Beijing that if its vessels don’t break contact with partners, costs will follow.
Cyber is a second channel for imposing costs. Beyond highlighting Chinese cyber actions against the US and its partners, the US can integrate offensive cyber capabilities into the ‘respond’ phase. By imposing proportionate costs on Chinese government, military or coast guard entities or networks, the US can signal that continued Chinese grey-zone actions will have consequences. For example, if a Chinese vessel rams a Philippine ship, the US could respond by disrupting critical systems associated with Chinese maritime operations. Because such capabilities can be employed from outside the immediate area of a dispute, they also provide strategic depth and another means of responding to Chinese coercion.
The US Coast Guard and Navy can work alongside partner coast guards to block, stop, and arrest militia or fishing crews caught operating illegally in partner waters. The principle is simple: partners enforce their own laws in their own waters, with US ships and intelligence backing them. This must stay strictly legal and be confined to those breaking international law and the law of US partners. Done properly, it turns Beijing’s favoured tactic, coercion dressed as law enforcement, back on itself, but from firmer legal ground.
Financial tools should be tied to response options. In 2022, the US Treasury sanctioned Chinese distant-water fishing companies , adding more than 150 vessels to the Specially Designated Nationals list over human rights abuses and illegal fishing. Extending that precedent to illegal fishing and militia activity within the region would mean freezing assets and persuading banks to cut their ties, further complicating militia and fishing operations and imposing additional costs.
The last two steps in the chain – exploiting and disseminating – are where the US holds its greatest advantage. It already operates extensively with regional partners, so the infrastructure for sharing information exists. It simply needs to be expanded to countries bullied by China.
That should include tracking data. If China can ram Philippine ships in Philippine waters, Manila should receive the information it needs to enforce its own rights, lawfully, in waters that Beijing claims. That should involve all of the aforementioned strategies supported by US capabilities – enforcing exclusive economic zones by arresting illegal fishing vessels, partnering with the US to jam Chinese drones within those areas, or using US intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance networks to identify and remove Chinese intelligence and surveillance sensors within partners’ territories.
A US–China hotline could accompany all of this, alerting Beijing before the response phase commences and giving it a chance to back down.
Critics will warn that all this would risk escalation, and in the short term some friction would be likely. But Beijing currently pays nothing for testing its neighbours, and it will keep testing them until it pays much more. Demonstrating resolve, rather than tacitly accepting Chinese sovereignty claims, is more likely to lead to de-escalation over time.
Additionally, many regional states dislike China’s bullying but lack the resources to resist it alone. Seeing Washington finally impose costs, lawfully and alongside partners, could stiffen the resolve of those fence-sitters. In grey-zone competition, passivity is a strategy that’s working in Beijing’s favour.
William ‘Billy’ Price is a Major in the United States Marine Corps Reserve, has deployed to the Middle East and Africa as an intelligence officer, and has a master’s in International Service from American University.

articles.title_orig: “That's just insane.” Elephant dies in South Africa – and scientists are stunned at what happens next
articles.title_zh: “That's just insane.” Elephant dies in South Africa – and scientists are stunned at what happens next
articles.content_orig:
Elephants continue to influence the savannah long after they die, new study finds.
In 2009, a large, lone elephant called Alexander died beside a road in South Africa’s Kruger National Park. Over the next few months, researcher Dave Thompson watched what happened to the carcass and wondered how it was affecting the savannah.
Now, research inspired by that thought has found that elephant carcasses can continue to shape ecosystems for years.
Thompson passed Alexander’s body regularly, en route to a different project. “Watching the decomposition of that carcass got me curious,” says Thompson, from the South African Environmental Observation Network. So, a project was born.
In life, elephants are ecosystem engineers . When they munch plants, fell trees, disperse seeds, fertilise the soil and trample the ground, they create opportunities for other species to thrive. But what happens to that influence when an elephant dies?
When a whale dies and sinks to the bottom of the ocean, its carcass can become a rich source of nutrients, sustaining life for decades. Thompson wondered if something similar was happening on land.
To find out, researchers studied elephant carcasses of different ages, measuring changes in the soil, microbes, plants and grazing animals around them. The results are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .
Initially, plant life was snuffed out. Nutrients from the body leached into the ground, affecting the soil chemistry. Around fresh carcasses, nitrogen concentrations were up to 3,000 times higher than normal. “That amount of ammonium was not on my bingo card,” says Tercia Midzi, who works at Kruger National Park. Levels were so high that plants struggled to grow.
Soil-dwelling bacteria were affected too. Although their diversity went down, the activity of those that survived rocketed, as a few fast-growing species became dominant.
Plants showed a similar pattern. Once the soil chemistry mellowed, plant diversity remained low, with a handful of nutritious, fast-growing species taking over. The carcass “turns these grasses from watery iceberg lettuce into a juicy romaine,” says Deron Burkepile from UC Santa Barbara.
This did not go unnoticed. Herbivores repeatedly returned to feed on the nutritious grasses, while their manure added yet more nutrients to the soil.
The effects persisted for at least eight years, revealing a previously overlooked way that elephants shape ecosystems.
“It was such a powerful reminder that what we see in nature is often shaped by legacies from the past,” says Izak Smit from South African National Parks, “even when the causes of those legacies have long since disappeared from view.”

articles.title_orig: Lindstrom, Polish, Sternfeld and Tabansky pushing for honors at World Para Series Stage 4
articles.title_zh: Lindstrom, Polish, Sternfeld and Tabansky pushing for honors at World Para Series Stage 4
articles.content_orig:
SANTIAGO, Chile – Four archers from the United States are this week in South America for Stage 4 of the inaugural Hyundai World Archery Para Series, which runs from Wednesday until Sunday.
Leading the U.S. team is 2024 Paralympic champion, Jason Tabansky (pictured above). He is joined in the W1 division by Ryan Lindstrom. Karen Sternfeld will look to continue her upward trajectory in para recurve women following appearances in Thailand, Czech Republic and India. The quartet is completed by three-time Paralympian, KJ Polish in para compound men.
Sternfeld has featured at all three previous stages, while Tabansky has competed at two and both Lindstrom and Polish at one. Tabansky took silver in Thailand back in April, before securing gold in Stage 2, held in Nove Mesto, Czech Republic.
Polish was top seed in compound men in Nove Mesto, before losing his quarterfinal contest to eventual bronze medalist, Nathan MacQueen (GBR), via a shootoff.
Sternfeld’s qualification scores have steadily improved throughout the year. She posted 462 in Thailand, before scoring 553 in Czech Republic and then 564 in India.
Lindstrom (pictured), meanwhile, registered a personal best score of 616 in qualification in Czech Republic. The 42-year-old from Florida is still relatively new to international archery. He only made the decision to compete after watching Tabansky win gold in Paris two years ago, and though a podium regular on the national circuit, Lindstrom is fully aware of what it will take to challenge internationally.
“The biggest difference to me is obviously the pressure turns up a bit but that's OK because it helps me focus,” he explained. “My two best scores were shot at international tournaments.
“Competing at this level I feel it truly solidifies the feeling that I'm competing with the best in the world rather than just showing up and shooting at a tournament. That's a really cool feeling.”
Lindstrom won bronze at the 142nd USA Target Nationals and silver at the 2026 U.S. Open, which took place in Springfield, Mo. in August. Since then, the focus has been finishing the year strong.
He added, “I have been using the rest of the outdoor season in the states as practice and training. I’ve been trying different techniques and equipment, including traveling to San Antonio to do some fine tuning, which I feel went really well.”
This is the fourth of five stages in the inaugural World Para Series. The fifth and final stage is in Dubai, UAE from December 5-10.
You can follow the scores, results and progress of the four U.S. archers, with medal matches taking place across Saturday and Sunday.
From Chile, all four USA archers head to Lima, Peru for the 2026 Para Pan American Championships, and a much larger U.S. consisting of 17 athletes. This event runs from October 21-27, with quota spots available for the 2027 Para Pan Am Games, which are also in Lima, Peru next August.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Rises, Nasdaq Slips to Start Begin Big Week of Earnings; Bond Market Closed Today

articles.content_orig:
Bank earnings kick off this week with no fewer than seven of the biggest names set to report. With the S&P 500 near all-time highs, the results could provide a significant market catalyst. Financials are the third-worst performing S&P 500 sector in 2026. Despite being flat on the year, the options market is pricing in some big moves as investor weigh the impact of higher rates and stretched consumer.
Here's what the options market sees, according to the latest Cboe LiveVol data. Goldman Sachs - Tuesday, Oct. 13
The options market is pricing in a 2.84% move for Goldman Sachs after it reports earnings. Across the last eight reported quarters, the stock has moved just about 2% on average. Only three of those quarters have seen a negative stock reaction, with the most recent being a 1.87% move lower in April. The stock rallied a whopping 9% after July's Q2 report, which is the largest post-earnings move since January, 2019. JPMorgan - Tuesday, Oct. 13
Options are pricing in a move similar to Goldman Sachs for JPMorgan, with a 2.5% implied move inline with its past eight quarter average of 2.22%. Unlike Goldman, JPMorgan's recent reports haven't been met with much positivity. The stock's 2.5% move higher following July's report was its first positive reaction since April, 2025, when it jumped 4% higher. Citigroup - Tuesday, Oct. 13
Citigroup heads into Tuesday's report up 11% on the year, best performance of any of this week's reporting names. Options are pricing in a tame 3% stock reaction in either direction, well below the 3.8% it has averaged across the last eight reported quarters. There is cause for pause, though. Last quarter, the stock surprised to the downside to the tune of 5.3% against a 3.5% implied move. Wells Fargo - Tuesday, Oct. 13
Wells Fargo rounds out Tuesday's big bank earnings as a name with a lot to prove. Not only is the stock down 10% this year, but it has also flunked its last three earnings reports, including a 5% move lower in April. This time around, options are implying a 3.5% move in either direction. That's well below its 5.6% average across the last eight quarters. Bank of America - Wednesday, Oct. 14
The options market thinks Bank of America might be able to sneak into positive territory on the year after Wednesday's report. A move higher would be its third-straight post-earnings win. The current implied stock move is 2.9% in either direction, meaningfully above the 1.8% swing it has averaged across its last eight reported quarters. Morgan Stanley - Wednesday, Oct. 14
This company has rarely put a foot wrong in its recent earnings history. The stock has only moved lower once in its last eight reported quarters, a 1.3% move lower in July, 2025. This time around, options are implying a 3% move in either direction, compared to its eight-quarter average of 4.3%. A move higher on Wednesday would make it five straight for Morgan Stanley. articles.title_orig: Resmetirom Tied to Lower MACE vs Semaglutide in Real-World MASLD Analysis
articles.title_zh: Resmetirom Tied to Lower MACE vs Semaglutide in Real-World MASLD Analysis
articles.content_orig:
A propensity-matched TriNetX analysis presented at ACG 2026 found lower MACE and mortality with resmetirom vs semaglutide over 2 years in MASLD/MASH.
Patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and hepatic fibrosis who received resmetirom had lower rates of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality than matched patients receiving semaglutide, according to findings from a real-world analysis presented at the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) 2026 Annual Scientific Meeting in Nashville, Tennessee. 1
The poster, presented by Jalal Samhoun, MD, Florida Atlantic University, addresses a gap the investigators identified: there are no comparative cardiovascular outcome data between the 2 therapies, even though cardiovascular disease contributes heavily to morbidity and mortality in MASLD and MASH. 1
Resmetirom is an oral, liver-directed, thyroid hormone receptor-β agonist. In March 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted it accelerated approval for noncirrhotic MASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis. It was the first drug approved for the disease. In the phase 3 MAESTRO-NASH trial, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 25.9% and 29.9% of patients receiving resmetirom 80 mg and 100 mg, respectively, versus 9.7% with placebo. Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol fell by 13.6% and 16.3% at week 24. 2
Semaglutide 2.4 mg received accelerated approval for the same population in August 2025 based on part 1 of the phase 3 ESSENCE trial, in which 62.9% of patients receiving semaglutide achieved steatohepatitis resolution without worsening of fibrosis, versus 34.3% with placebo. 3 Unlike resmetirom, semaglutide has a dedicated cardiovascular outcome trial. In SELECT, it reduced MACE by 20% versus placebo in adults with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity without diabetes. 4
Investigators used the TriNetX Global Collaborative Network to identify adults with MASLD or MASH and hepatic fibrosis receiving resmetirom or semaglutide. They performed 1:1 propensity score matching on demographics, cardiovascular risk factors, metabolic comorbidities, liver disease characteristics, medications, and laboratory values. 1
The final cohorts included 4253 patients each. The primary outcome was MACE, defined as myocardial infarction (MI), ischemic stroke, or all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were all-cause mortality, MI, atrial fibrillation (AF), and heart failure (HF) . 1
At 1 year, resmetirom was associated with lower risks of MACE (hazard ratio [HR], 0.50; 95% CI, 0.32-0.80; P = .003), all-cause mortality (HR, 0.29; 95% CI, 0.16-0.54; P <.001), and HF (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.42-0.99; P = .04). The 2 groups did not differ significantly in MI or AF. 1
At 2 years, the lower risks of MACE (HR, 0.61; 95% CI, 0.41-0.89; P = .01) and all-cause mortality (HR, 0.33; 95% CI, 0.20-0.55; P <.001) persisted. AF showed a nonsignificant trend favoring resmetirom (HR, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.41-1.07; P = .09), and MI rates remained similar. 1
Investigators described the findings as early real-world evidence that resmetirom may confer cardiovascular benefits beyond its established hepatic effects. The lower risks they observed emerged within the first year and persisted through 2 years of follow-up. 1
The analysis is retrospective and drew on electronic health records, so it can show associations but cannot establish causation. Propensity matching accounts only for variables recorded in the database, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. All-cause mortality was included in the MACE composite, while rates of MI did not differ between groups.1 Additionally, semaglutide has shown cardiovascular benefit in a randomized trial, but no randomized cardiovascular outcome data for resmetirom have been published. 2,4

articles.title_orig: Data centres are turning Trump voters into Democrats
articles.title_zh: Data centres are turning Trump voters into Democrats
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, there weren't many voters talking about data centers. Now, the massive facilities being built to satisfy the enormous computing needs of the AI boom have become one of the most explosive issues of the 2026 midterms , and their construction is opening a divide between the Trump administration and Republicans running in state and federal races this fall.
When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, most data centers were being built in blue states. But by 2025, 68% of data centers online were in red states. Now, 75% of data centers under construction and 80% of data centers in the planning stage are in predominantly Republican states, according to new data from Cleanview Research, an independent energy market intelligence company tracking data center development.
"Red states have more of a history of accepting large, energy intensive, infrastructure projects — even those that might have detrimental effects on communities," said Chris Millay, a data center analyst at the macroeconomic consultancy Greenmantle. He also points to the relative lack of environmental regulation and the availability of open land as reasons rural states are receiving more investment.
President Trump sees the AI race as critical to the economy and national security, and he's one of data centers' biggest boosters. At a recent Ohio rally, he said of data centers, "We want them … look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio — you can't just turn them off. They'll go to China."
He has repeatedly dismissed public opposition to data centers, posting on Truth Social that "the only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor." Mr. Trump has also resisted regulation, though he has called on developers to give back to local communities through education, lower taxes, job creation and energy cost protections.
Red states may be hosting most of the boom, and increasingly, communities living next to data centers are pushing back. People who live near data centers have reported concerns about their property values, noise , higher energy bills and resource depletion. Meanwhile, calls for moratoriums are spreading through communities across the country.
Overall, opposition to data centers outweighs support by 30 points, with polls showing the majority of Republicans oppose the construction of data centers near them.
"It's such a consensus issue it's really impossible to take the other side," said Millay. "When voters see a politician who supports data centers, they think, 'Well, how am I going to trust him with my job?'"
Some of the president's closest allies have begun to break with him on the issue. In Texas, which has the most data centers under construction, GOP Gov. Greg Abbott has paused environmental permits and grid connections for new data centers. Abbott, who is seeking a fourth term, is in a surprisingly close race against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.
In Texas' tight Senate race , the Republican nominee, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, wants to end Texas' sales tax break for data centers. He has also said they should be held criminally liable if they power AI chatbots that endanger children.
Data centers seem to be the single issue where Democratic and Republican candidates sound nearly identical.
In Ohio, Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor, said in a press release, "I am calling on our Statehouse to pass a conditional moratorium on data centers."
Her GOP opponent, Vivek Ramaswamy, has gone further. He vowed to "issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio," and to keep that pause in place until lawmakers pass his "Ohioans-First" law, which would require data centers to provide free electricity to surrounding residents.
A recent New York Times/Siena poll found that data centers are a weak point for Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, with voters favoring his opponent by an 11-point margin on the issue.
Campaigns have spent $45 million this year on ads that mention data centers — most of them in opposition — according to AdImpact.
In Georgia, where candidates have spent nearly $13 million on ads mentioning data centers — more than any other state — the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Rick Jackson, is sticking with Mr. Trump. While the Democratic candidate, Keisha Lance Bottoms, is calling for a temporary moratorium on construction, Jackson says the decision should be left up to local officials.
Jackson made the case for data centers at a recent press conference, saying he wanted "to educate people on the benefit if they want [a data center]." Some counties, he said, expect they "will have zero property taxes after the data center goes in." Effingham County, where OpenAI plans a $20 billion data center, has pledged to use some of that revenue to cut homeowners' property taxes.
Because most of the next wave of data centers is largely planned in states Mr. Trump won in 2024, the choices Republican candidates make, siding with voters or with the president, could decide whether those projects are paused, made more expensive or even canceled.

articles.title_orig: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.title_zh: First Impressions: Dell XPS Googlebook and the Googlebook OS
articles.content_orig:
Posted on October 12, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 16 Comments
As someone who has, over the years, found himself deep in the Google ecosystem of hardware and services, I had been curious about the Googlebook concept for a while — whether it would be basically a fancy Chromebook, or if it would offer something more, and more useful , than that line of affordable but mostly limited laptops. When the Googlebook models were announced in September, I decided to go ahead and pre-order one: The Acer Googlebook 14.
It turns out, however, that apparently lots of people had the same idea as me. Best Buy sent me an email telling me that despite taking my pre-order money, the Acer was out of stock and they didn’t know when they would get more. I cancelled that order and went with the Dell XPS Googlebook instead, which, I think by virtue of being $100 more expensive than the Acer, was in stock. It arrived the day after I ordered it — and when, alas, I was away at New York Comic Con for a few days. I finally got a chance to set it up and play with it yesterday.
My first impressions: It’s pretty nice! Also, Google still has work to do on its shiny new operating system.
Hardware first: The XPS Googlebook is a really nice little laptop. It’s physically the smallest of the five Googlebooks available at launch (the other four coming from Acer, Asus, Hewlett-Packard and Lenovo). It’s clearly meant to be in the “ultrabook” category of laptop, which is to say, light and thin and not terribly concerned with ports (it comes with two USB-C ports and that’s it — not even a headphone jack). It’s also the only Googlebook at launch that does not come with an OLED screen, although the screen it has is perfectly nice and the blacks are certainly inky enough for government work.
All of the launch Googlebooks were required by Google to have certain minimum hardware: at least 16GB of RAM, high-speed processors, either by Intel or Qualcomm (the XPS comes with a Snapdragon X Elite), 512GB SSD, a metal, not plastic, chassis, backlit keyboard, and a touchscreen with a high refresh rate (120 Hz here). None of this comes cheap these days, and the initial set of Googlebooks are priced between $899 and $1299, with the XPS I got coming in at $999. This is more expensive than just about any Chromebook, more expensive than the new Macbook Neo, and on par with a newish Macbook Air.
The minimum requirements pay off, at least for the XPS. It feels really solid for such a small computer, and everything about it looks and feels nice. The keyboard has a nice snap to it and has almost no flex, the screen as mentioned is very good (and comes with an anti-glare coating, which is a feature I appreciate now that I have it), and while it has fans, which turned on while I was setting up the laptop, they are quiet and barely noticeable when they’re on, which so far has only been during that setup.
As mentioned the processor here is a Snapdragon chip rather than an Intel one, and that’s fine because Android (which the Googlebook OS is based on, and which, frankly, it’s mostly just a reskinned version of) is designed to run on ARM chips, which Snapdragon is. Everything runs quickly so far, and ARM chips are typically meant to be more efficient than x86 chips like Intel’s, although so far the battery life I’ve seen out of the XPS is good but not amazing.
The XPS has quirks — the keyboard is a modified Chromebook set-up, which means the Caps button is a “search” button first (you can make it a Caps button by holding down the shift button, which defeats the whole purpose of a caps button), and there’s a “Google” button on the bottom row which opens an app drawer or can be used to access the “magic pointer” (more on that later). Also, the speakers, while perfectly acceptable, make the chassis vibrate, particularly the trackpad, which is a not entirely pleasant feeling. The trackpad is mechanical, not haptic, and the click does take some pressure (it responds to taps perfectly well). The I/O situation as mentioned is sparse, but inasmuch as I already have a MacBook Air, which also only has two USB-C ports, I am already well-acquainted with the dongle life, and I have bluetooth headphones. I’m not going to give the XPS too much crap for that.
So as a piece of hardware, the XPS is solid. Now, how is the software — the Googlebook operating system and all the “AI” bells and whistles that Google has piled on top of it?
As a preface, I should note that I knew going into this that as an early adopter of this platform, I would essentially be a beta tester for it, since almost no 1.0 release of anything survives its first encounter with users out in the world. In the week since Googlebooks have hit the market there have already been updates to the OS to fix bugs and other flubs. So I’m okay with having a little patience in this shake-down cruise. That said, being patient doesn’t mean not pointing out the flaws that do currently exist.
One of those flaws is that at the moment the Googlebook is doing a crap job at one of its marquee features, namely, integration with Android phones, where one is supposed to be able to connect laptop and phone seamlessly, stream apps from the phone to the laptop, hand off work from one to the other, and drop files from one into the other painlessly. As a Pixel phone owner, this promised integration was a huge inducement to try out the Googlebook — I wanted what (presumably) iPhone users have with their Macs. It would, in fact, be really useful. And as a Pixel owner running Android 17, I am someone best positioned to get that integration right out of the box.
Except that the Googlebook keeps dropping its connection to my phone and not being able to find it after that, unless I restart both the phone and the Googlebook. It happens when I take my phone away from the laptop and/or close the laptop, breaking the connection between the two. A short disconnect doesn’t seem to be a problem; a longer one seems to flummox it entirely. I believe this is a known issue that’s being addressed, so that’s good. But it’s still annoying right now . I don’t want to have to keep resetting my laptop and phone to get the promised integration.
(I’ve also noticed that phone apps streamed onto the Googlebook can have choppy scrolling, although I don’t know if that’s a problem with the integration or an artifact of my occasionally-janky internet connection.)
That said, when the integration does work, it’s pretty neat, and I see it being really useful when I’m working on my laptop and need something from my phone, or want to access an app that I don’t have running natively on my computer. As mentioned already, the Googlebook OS is pretty much a reskinned version of Android 17, so all the apps that run on an Android phone should run just fine on the laptop (there are apps that apparently struggle on the Intel Googlebooks, but even there something like 97% of apps run perfectly well). During the setup, if you pair your Googlebook with your phone it will install the apps you have there over to the laptop, so you’ll be able to run them natively even if you can’t access your phone. But they are different instances of the app, so streaming an app might still come in handy.
So: Great in concept! Execution still needs work.
Google is going all in on “AI” integration on the Googlebooks, making sure that Gemini, its in-house “AI,” is only a click, button-mash or cursor wiggle away, the latter being the “magic pointer” feature. You can invoke Gemini and ask it about what’s on your screen, or have it smoosh two images you have into a single “AI”-ified picture and so on (the Googlebooks also come with an offer for an entire year of the “Pro” level of Gemini, which comes with five terabytes of cloud storage, which is arguably more useful). The point is, no matter where you go on the Googlebook OS, Gemini is right there, lurking, waiting for you to do something with it.
